items.title: L’agriculture, ciment de l’Europe ?
items.description: L'agriculture a été l’un des piliers de la construction européenne, si ce n’est son principal ciment. Contrairement au charbon et à l’acier, elle concernait l’ensemble des pays fondateurs. Elle a toujours occupé une place centrale dans la perception des populations, puisque personne n’échappe aux enjeux alimentaires. C’était déjà vrai il y a 70 ans. Lorsque l’on évoque l’agriculture et la construction européenne, on parle d’une aventure de longue durée, qui s’étend sur plusieurs décennies. Depuis 70 ans, l’Europe a renforcé ses productions agricoles. Au lendemain de la Seconde Guerre mondiale, la situation alimentaire était catastrophique et les tickets de rationnement ont perduré longtemps dans de nombreux pays, y compris en France. Au-delà de la sécurité alimentaire, le développement agricole a également facilité l’aménagement du territoire, l’inclusion des espaces ruraux et, progressivement, la préservation des paysages. Il a aussi contribué à garantir la sécurité sanitaire des aliments consommés en Europe. La puissance normative européenne demeure très importante dans ce domaine. Ces normes ont inspiré une partie du monde, en particulier ces dernières années, avec l’intégration de considérations environnementales plus ambitieuses. La politique agricole commune (PAC) a accompagné beaucoup plus de jeunes Européens que le programme Erasmus. En sept décennies, elle a largement contribué à sécuriser le quotidien des populations européennes. Dans le même temps, la PAC a régulièrement constitué un sujet de friction lors des élargissements. Le Royaume-Uni a beaucoup négocié sur cette question, ainsi que sur la pêche. Lorsque l’Espagne et le Portugal ont rejoint la Communauté dans les années 1980, les sujets agricoles étaient déjà une source de tensions aux frontières pyrénéennes. De nombreux débats ont également eu lieu lors du passage de l’Europe à 27, puis à 28 États membres : il fallait répartir un budget européen plus important, dont un tiers est aujourd’hui encore consacré à la PAC, après avoir longtemps représenté les deux tiers. En définitive, sur les 70 années de construction européenne, la majeure partie du budget de l’Union a servi à garantir aux Européens un approvisionnement alimentaire suffisant, de qualité et diversifié, même si ce choix a parfois suscité des controverses. L’Europe agricole : les paradoxes d’une politique commune L’histoire de l’Europe agricole a été marquée par plusieurs épisodes emblématiques : les excédents de production dans les années 1980, puis les changements de politique économique, avec l’abandon progressif des quotas dans les années 1990 et 2000. L’agriculture européenne s’est alors ouverte à la mondialisation et aux échanges internationaux, à l’instar de l’économie européenne dans son ensemble. Avec le temps, cette évolution a fait apparaître plusieurs paradoxes. Dès le début des années 1990, la PAC a engagé des réformes structurelles visant à mieux prendre en compte l’environnement, notamment sous l’impulsion de Jacques Chirac et d’une France alors influente dans le concert européen. La politique agricole s’est progressivement et davantage tournée vers les enjeux environnementaux et moins vers la production. Parallèlement, elle est devenue moins commune et plus concurrentielle entre les États membres. Enfin, l’Europe dispose d’une politique agricole commune en matière d’organisation des marchés et de normes, mais ne mène pas de politique agricole extérieure véritablement commune. En dehors des frontières de l’Union, chaque État membre agit largement à sa manière. Il participe aux accords commerciaux européens, mais promeut ses productions, mène sa diplomatie économique et valorise ses produits à l’échelle mondiale à travers un discours souvent marqué par une identité nationale. Les réflexions sur l’Europe comme puissance n’ont donc jamais intégré les questions agricoles et alimentaires à la hauteur de leur importance. L’Europe a beaucoup mobilisé l’agriculture pour unir ses États membres et ses sociétés, mais elle a peiné à s’exprimer de manière unifiée à l’extérieur, comme c’est souvent le cas dans d’autres domaines de la politique internationale. L’avenir de la PAC : entre opportunités et inquiétudes Ces dernières années, l’Europe semble se chercher. En interne, elle peut susciter de la lassitude, du découragement ou de la frustration. Il est toutefois important de rappeler les effets positifs qu’elle produit, notamment en matière de mobilité et de facilitation des échanges de produits, de personnes et de capitaux. On observe également, dans plusieurs pays européens, la montée de mouvements nationalistes et de critiques à l’égard de l’Europe. Sur la scène européenne, l’agriculture a évolué en parallèle de ces transformations politiques. La dernière réforme de la PAC, adoptée avec en parallèle la sortie de pandémie de Covid-19, a notamment renforcé le principe de subsidiarité en permettant à chaque État membre d’élaborer son propre plan stratégique national agricole. C’était une première depuis le début de la construction européenne. Pour cette politique, l’une des rares à être véritablement communautaires, les États membres ont donc obtenu une plus grande latitude pour renationaliser certaines pratiques. Cette tendance devrait s’accentuer lors de la prochaine étape. Le prochain cadre financier pluriannuel donnera aux États membres une marge de manœuvre accrue dans la gestion de leur part du budget européen. La PAC, qui restera un élément important de ce budget, sera concernée à la fois par la transformation de l’ingénierie financière européenne et par sa propre réforme, actuellement en discussion, qui pourrait renforcer encore les logiques nationales. Le prochain cadre financier pluriannuel, pour la période 2028-2034, sera très différent. Ursula von der Leyen défend l’idée d’accorder davantage de souplesse et de manœuvre budgétaire dans un contexte d’accélération de l’agenda international qui n’est de fait plus en adéquation avec la fixation de règles sur sept ans. La PAC sera donc affectée à la fois par cette évolution financière et par sa propre réforme. Le mouvement engagé lors de la dernière réforme, il y a six ans, devrait ainsi s’amplifier. Les dernières déclarations du chancelier allemand conditionnent tout débat budgétaire sur le cadre financier pluriannuel à la question de l'aide budgétaire à l’Ukraine. Les négociations budgétaires entre États membres deviennent extrêmement complexes. Plusieurs pays, dont l’Allemagne et plusieurs États du Nord, plaident pour davantage de rigueur et une réduction de l’enveloppe globale. Si l’on tient compte de l’inflation, le budget de la prochaine PAC pourrait diminuer de 20 % par rapport à son niveau actuel. Dans tous les pays européens, la prochaine PAC suscite donc des inquiétudes. Il convient toutefois de nuancer ce constat : dans plusieurs pays, les agriculteurs ne souhaitent plus nécessairement bénéficier de la PAC telle qu’elle existe aujourd’hui. Certains estiment qu’elle freine les transitions, l’innovation et l’entrepreneuriat, et qu’elle sert essentiellement à maintenir la paix sociale dans les territoires ruraux à court terme. Selon eux, la PAC tend à freiner les performances agricoles, qu’elles soient écologiques ou économiques. Un certain nombre d’agriculteurs, davantage tournés vers l’entrepreneuriat et l’innovation, considèrent qu’elle contribue au maintien du statu quo dans une partie du monde agricole. Il faut cependant rappeler que, dans de nombreux États membres, la PAC constitue aussi la principale source de revenus et de sécurité pour les exploitations et les productions agricoles. Le monde agricole se fracture ainsi en deux dans l’ensemble des pays. Cette fracture est particulièrement nette en France, mais elle est également très présente ailleurs. En Italie, par exemple, de nombreuses manifestations agricoles ont eu lieu dans le sud du pays, avec des comportements qui reflètent les deux tendances évoquées. Nous sommes donc confrontés à un débat budgétaire et à une réflexion sur la nature de la PAC : ce qu’elle est aujourd’hui, ce qu’elle pourrait cesser d’être et ce qu’elle devrait financer en priorité. Plusieurs acteurs la remettent fortement en question. L’Ukraine au cœur de l’équation agricole européenne Le rôle de l’Ukraine constitue un élément majeur de l’équation agricole européenne. Comme le suggère notre ouvrage Russie – Ukraine : la guerre hybride , co-écrit avec Thierry Pouch et Arthur Portier, la question agricole pèsera lourdement sur l’évolution des relations entre l’Ukraine et l’Europe. L’Ukraine ne rejoindra pas l’Union européenne en renonçant à son agriculture, l’un de ses principaux atouts économiques et géopolitiques. La PAC, dans sa forme actuelle, ne correspond toutefois pas à l’identité agricole ukrainienne, qui repose sur une production très importante, une forte orientation vers l’exportation et une grande intensité capitalistique. Par ailleurs, l’Europe redoute les conséquences de l’adhésion de l’Ukraine, qui modifierait encore davantage l’équilibre budgétaire et la répartition des crédits de la PAC, alors que son enveloppe pourrait déjà diminuer. Or l’Ukraine possède probablement l’agriculture la plus compétitive du continent européen. Les coûts de production y sont très inférieurs à ceux de la France. Ainsi, si l’Ukraine rejoint l’Union, l’écart de compétitivité entre les productions sera considérable. L’Ukraine dispose également, malgré les pertes territoriales subies, d’un espace agricole immense, de sols d’une qualité exceptionnelle et d’un tissu d’acteurs économiques qui continue de monter en puissance malgré la guerre. Il faut aussi prendre en compte les progrès accomplis par le secteur agricole ukrainien depuis cinq ans : il fait preuve à la fois de résilience et d’innovation, et ne se limite plus à produire des matières premières destinées à l’exportation. Son industrie agroalimentaire se développe rapidement et produit des biens transformés à plus forte valeur ajoutée. L’Ukraine peut également contribuer à répondre à un besoin important de l’Europe : celle-ci a adopté de vastes stratégies de transition climatique et énergétique afin de sortir du pétrole, mais ne produit pas suffisamment de biomasse agricole à des fins énergétiques. Pour réduire notre dépendance au pétrole, il faudra davantage de ressources agricoles. Une part importante de certains carburants européens est déjà issue de biocarburants. Le carburant aérien durable, ou « sustainable aviation fuel », en est un exemple révélateur. D’ici 2035, les compagnies aériennes européennes devront intégrer une part importante de produits agricoles à leurs carburants. Les secteurs agricoles seront donc appelés à contribuer au transport aérien de demain. Il faut davantage de biomasse agricole, mais l’Europe n’en produit pas assez. L’Ukraine accélère actuellement le développement de cultures intermédiaires ou non alimentaires pour contribuer à cette production, comme le font déjà le Brésil, l’Inde, l’Indonésie et la Malaisie, notamment. Ces pays investissent de plus en plus dans l’agriculture pour réduire leur dépendance au pétrole, et pas uniquement pour assurer leur approvisionnement alimentaire. Ils cherchent également à concilier cette démarche avec les engagements pris dans le cadre de l’accord de Paris. L’Union européenne est donc mise au défi sur ce terrain. La compétitivité agricole et agroalimentaire européenne Comme les décisions ne sont que rarement prises à 27, l’Europe perd en influence et en capacité à s’exprimer sur la scène mondiale. Pourtant, lorsqu’on agrège les statistiques des 27 États membres, l’agriculture et l’agroalimentaire européens sont puissants. C’est un peu comme aux Jeux olympiques : si l’on additionne les médailles des 27 États membres, l’Europe se classe en tête. Mais, pris individuellement, les pays ont une place beaucoup plus limitée sur la scène internationale. La France traverse actuellement une période charnière dans les secteurs agricole et agroalimentaire. Sa situation est moins favorable qu’il y a quelques années, notamment parce qu’elle a largement délaissé le marché européen. Elle reste forte, voire parfois plus forte, sur certaines destinations lointaines, mais son influence dans les négociations politiques et budgétaires à Bruxelles a diminué. Par ailleurs, le centre de gravité de l’innovation agricole s’est déplacé vers l’est de l’Europe, notamment vers la Pologne, qui a beaucoup progressé au cours des quinze dernières années. La France a surtout perdu des parts de marché dans l’Union européenne. Sa balance commerciale demeure très excédentaire hors du marché communautaire, mais elle a enregistré l’an dernier un déficit de 5 milliards d’euros vis-à-vis des autres pays européens. L’Italie, le Danemark et l’Espagne ont, au contraire, gagné des parts de marché au détriment de la France ces dernières années. Le monde agricole français, dans toute sa diversité, risque donc de voir l’influence politique de la France décliner dans les prochains mois. La capacité du pays à peser sur le budget et à défendre le maintien de la PAC pourrait être plus faible que jamais dans l’histoire de la construction européenne. Rappelons également que le versement de la contribution d’un État à l’Union européenne est lié à des conditions qui déterminent sa capacité à recevoir des aides communautaires, notamment celles de la PAC. Enfin, l’Union européenne doit faire face à des menaces extérieures, notamment à des formes d’attaques hybrides. Vous avez peut-être entendu parler des incidents visant des supermarchés en Europe. Ils ne sont pas les seuls concernés : de nombreuses entreprises et industries agroalimentaires ont également été touchées, notamment dans le secteur des produits de la mer et, plus largement, dans les chaînes du froid. Les acteurs de ces secteurs sont victimes de cyberattaques. Les menaces hybrides prennent aussi des formes plus concrètes : sabotage de sites industriels, mobilisations visant parfois des exploitations agricoles, des zones d’élevage ou des industries agroalimentaires, dans le but de ralentir ou de perturber les activités logistiques. À cela s’ajoute une désinformation multicanale particulièrement importante sur ces questions. L’agriculture européenne est également mise à l’épreuve par les chocs géopolitiques, logistiques et maritimes mondiaux, ainsi que par les changements climatiques sur le continent. Nous avons longtemps considéré, à tort, que l’Europe serait à l’abri de ces bouleversements et qu’ils concerneraient surtout d’autres régions du monde. L’agriculture européenne devra apprendre des expériences de nombreuses régions confrontées à la rareté de l’eau et aux difficultés de maintenir leur production dans un contexte d’instabilité croissante. En matière d’agroécologie, les Européens auront donc beaucoup à apprendre des autres régions du monde, plutôt que l’inverse. C’est un exemple de cette diplomatie inversée qui se développe. L’article L’agriculture, ciment de l’Europe ? est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: Learn about the 8 personalities, landmarks, and symbols featured on the new Heritage Cedi notes
items.description: From Ghana’s first President, Dr Kwame Nkrumah, featured on the GH¢200 note, to renowned Accra market trader Agnes Oforiwa Tagoe-Quarcoopome on the GH¢1 note, the Bank of Ghana’s new Heritage Series celebrates eight personalities whose contributions have helped shape the country’s history. The new Ghana cedi banknotes feature eight notable Ghanaian personalities on their front designs, alongside historic landmarks and traditional Adinkra symbols that reflect different aspects of the country’s heritage. President John Dramani Mahama officially unveiled the Heritage Series at the Bank of Ghana’s Bank Square headquarters in Accra on Thursday. The new notes are expected to enter circulation on 1 December 2026 and will be used alongside the existing banknotes, which will remain legal tender. Each denomination has a distinct theme, with a prominent national figure featured on the front and a landmark or historical site on the reverse. An accompanying Adinkra symbol represents the central message or value associated with each note. The Bank of Ghana says the designs bring together national heroes, historic sites, monuments and Adinkra symbols to reflect the country’s history, identity and cultural values. Although the personalities and landmarks differ, all eight denominations share a common design layout. The front features the Bank of Ghana’s name, the denomination written in words, the national coat of arms and the black star, alongside a column of Adinkra symbols next to the portrait. The reverse of each note also features a QR code and decorative borders inspired by traditional kente patterns. Here is a closer look at the personalities, landmarks and symbols featured on each denomination. GH¢1: Agnes Oforiwa Tagoe-Quarcoopome (Commerce) The grey GH¢1 banknote honours Agnes Oforiwa Tagoe-Quarcoopome (1913–1997), an Accra-based market woman and trader remembered for her support for Kwame Nkrumah’s independence campaign. The back shows market women selling foodstuffs, representing the important role of women in commerce and the everyday activities that sustain the economy. The accompanying Adinkra symbol is Bese Saka, meaning a sack of kola nuts. The symbol represents abundance, wealth, unity, and commercial prosperity. GH¢2: Cardinal Peter Dery (Religious Freedom) The orange-and-gold GH¢2 note features Cardinal Peter Poreku Dery (1918–2008), the former Catholic Archbishop of Tamale who became Ghana’s first cardinal in 2006. The reverse of the note features the Larabanga Mosque in the Savannah Region, a historic mud-and-timber structure widely regarded as one of the oldest mosques in West Africa. Its Adinkra symbol is Nyame Dua, meaning “tree of God”. It represents God’s presence, protection, and spiritual guidance. GH¢5: Dr J.E.K. Aggrey (Education) The blue GH¢5 note celebrates James Emman Kwegyir Aggrey (1875–1927), one of Ghana’s most respected educationists and intellectuals. The reverse features the clock-tower building of Achimota School in Accra, an institution he helped establish and which remains one of Ghana’s prominent educational institutions. The Adinkra symbol on the note is Nea Onnim No Sua A, Ohu, which means “one who does not know can know by learning”. It highlights the importance of education, knowledge, and lifelong learning. GH¢10: Justice Annie Jiagge (Justice and Equality) The green GH¢10 note honours Justice Annie Jiagge (1918–1996), a pioneering Ghanaian judge and women’s rights advocate who made significant contributions to the advancement of justice and gender equality. The reverse features the Supreme Court of Ghana, with the Martyrs of the Rule of Law monument standing in front of the building. The note carries the Adinkra symbol Epa, meaning handcuffs, which represents law, justice, and the enforcement of legal principles. GH¢20: Dr Ephraim Amu (Arts and Entertainment) The purple GH¢20 note features Dr Ephraim Amu (1899–1995), a renowned Ghanaian composer, musicologist, and cultural figure. The reverse of the note features the National Theatre in Accra, an important centre for the country’s performing arts and cultural activities. Its distinctive architecture, with a roof resembling a ship, makes it one of the capital’s notable landmarks. The accompanying Adinkra symbol is Dono, representing the traditional talking drum. It is associated with praise, goodwill, communication, and rhythm, reflecting the importance of music and cultural expression. GH¢50: Theodosia Okoh (Nationalism) The red-orange GH¢50 note celebrates Theodosia Okoh (1922–2015), the Ghanaian artist and designer who created the country’s national flag. The reverse features Jubilee House, the official seat of the President of Ghana. The building’s architectural design draws inspiration from the traditional Akan stool, a symbol of authority and leadership. The Adinkra symbol is Fawohodie, which represents independence, freedom, and emancipation. GH¢100: Kofi Annan (Peace) The turquoise GH¢100 note honours Kofi Annan (1938–2018), Ghana’s internationally acclaimed diplomat and the seventh Secretary-General of the United Nations. The reverse features the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC) in Accra, an institution that provides training and research for military personnel, police officers, and civilians involved in peacekeeping and conflict management across Africa. The note carries the Adinkra symbol Bi Nka Bi, meaning “no one should bite another”. The symbol promotes peace, harmony, restraint, and peaceful coexistence. GH¢200: Dr Kwame Nkrumah (Sovereignty) The pink-and-red GH¢200 note features Dr Kwame Nkrumah (1909–1972), Ghana’s first President and the leader who guided the country to independence from British colonial rule on 6 March 1957. The reverse of the highest denomination features the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park in Accra, which houses his mausoleum and statue in honour of his contribution to Ghana’s independence and development. Its Adinkra symbol is Adinkrahene, often described as the chief of all Adinkra symbols. It represents greatness, leadership, authority, and charisma. The Bank of Ghana’s Heritage Series is expected to enter circulation on December 1. The new banknotes will circulate alongside the existing series, which will remain legal tender. The Bank has also urged the public to handle the new notes with care. It has cautioned against spraying, crumpling, or stapling the banknotes, as well as using them to make money bouquets.

items.title: PNCD 2026-2030 : le Gabon se dote d’un guide pour évaluer ses politiques publiques
items.description: Présenté officiellement le 11 novembre à Libreville, le Guide national de suivi et d'évaluation des politiques publiques doit harmoniser les méthodes de contrôle de l'action gouvernementale. Élaboré par le Commissariat général au plan avec l'appui du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD), cet instrument accompagne la mise en œuvre du PNCD 2026-2030. Pour sa véritable mise en œuvre, le PNCD bénéficie désormais d'un Guide national de suivi et d'évaluation pour « suivre et évaluer les projets et programmes » qui y sont contenus. © GabonReview Le gouvernement entend renforcer le contrôle de l'exécution des politiques publiques. À Libreville, le Commissariat général au plan a officiellement présenté, mercredi 11 novembre, le Guide national de suivi et d'évaluation des politiques publiques, un nouvel outil destiné à améliorer le pilotage des investissements et des projets de développement. Élaboré avec l'appui du Programme des Nations unies pour le développement (PNUD), ce document s'inscrit dans le cadre du Plan national de croissance et de développement (PNCD) 2026-2030. Il propose un cadre méthodologique commun pour harmoniser les pratiques de suivi, mesurer les résultats obtenus et apprécier l'efficacité des interventions publiques. L'ambition affichée est notamment de limiter les investissements improductifs, souvent qualifiés d'éléphants blancs, en renforçant les mécanismes de contrôle et de redevabilité. Les administrations responsabilisées La coordination du dispositif sera assurée par le ministère de la Planification et de la Prospective, en collaboration avec les ministères sectoriels. Cette organisation prévoit une harmonisation des outils, une consolidation des informations et un accompagnement technique des équipes chargées du suivi des projets. Chaque administration demeurera toutefois responsable de l'exécution de ses investissements et de la fiabilité des données transmises. Le suivi-évaluation est ainsi appelé à devenir un instrument de pilotage régulier, et non plus un simple exercice administratif intervenant après la réalisation des projets. La culture du résultat en ligne de mire La présentation du guide sera suivie d'un programme de formation destiné aux différentes parties prenantes afin de garantir une appropriation effective de cet outil. Cette réforme répond à un enjeu majeur du PNCD : améliorer le taux d'exécution des investissements publics et s'assurer que les ressources mobilisées produisent des résultats mesurables. Reste désormais à faire de ce dispositif un véritable instrument de contrôle de la dépense publique et de responsabilisation des administrations. L’article PNCD 2026-2030 : le Gabon se dote d'un guide pour évaluer ses politiques publiques est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: États-Unis : le patron de Nvidia Jensen Huang démissionne suite aux scandales
items.description: Le patron de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, a démissionné jeudi 12 novembre de son poste de directeur général, mettant fin à 33 années passées à la tête du groupe, après des révélations sur deux relations extraconjugales, dont l'une avec une femme accusée d'espionnage au profit de la Chine. Le conseil d'administration de Nvidia a indiqué que le PDG quitte également ses fonctions de président et d'administrateur, avec effet immédiat.

items.title: GNV obtient la certification ISO 50001 pour son système de management de l’énergie
items.description: GNV, compagnie de ferries du Groupe MSC, a obtenu la certification ISO 50001:2018 pour son Système de management de l’énergie. Cette reconnaissance, délivrée par l’organisme indépendant LRQA, couvre le siège de Gênes, l’atelier et 22 unités de la flotte, et atteste de l’adoption d’une approche structurée de la gestion de l’énergie, qui concerne les activités à terre comme à bord. La certification a été officiellement remise lors d’une rencontre au siège de GNV à Gênes, en présence de représentants de la Compagnie et de LRQA. La norme atteste de l’ adoption d’un système structuré de suivi des consommations énergétiques , d’analyse des performances et d’identification continue de nouvelles opportunités d’optimisation. Pour GNV, il s’agit de consolider la gestion de l’énergie dans les processus de l’entreprise, à terre comme à bord, selon une méthode d’amélioration continue. Cette étape fait suite à la certification ISO 14001 du Système de management environnemental, obtenue en 2025, et complète un ensemble de systèmes de management de plus en plus intégrés, orientés vers la maîtrise et la réduction de l’impact des activités de la Compagnie. Sur le plan industriel, la certification s’accompagne d’un programme de renouvellement de la flotte de plus de 1,3 milliard d’euros, qui prévoit l’arrivée de huit nouveaux navires d’ici fin 2029, dont six fonctionnant au GNL. Le plan est déjà à mi-parcours : GNV Polaris, GNV Orion, GNV Virgo et GNV Aurora sont déjà en service. GNV Virgo et GNV Aurora, les deux premières unités au GNL, permettent de réduire les émissions de CO₂ jusqu’à 50 % par unité transportable par rapport aux navires de génération précédente. Comme toutes les nouvelles constructions, elles sont équipées de systèmes de réduction catalytique sélective (SCR) et de technologies de récupération de chaleur, conformément aux exigences IMO Tier III et EEDI Phase II, et sont prééquipées pour le cold ironing. Le renouvellement se poursuit en parallèle sur les navires déjà en service, avec des interventions et des solutions technologiques visant à améliorer l’efficacité énergétique et à optimiser les processus de bord. Concernant le cold ironing, qui permet aux navires d’éteindre leurs générateurs à quai et de se raccorder au réseau électrique du port, les premiers tests ont été lancés sur deux ferries de la flotte, en France et en Espagne. « Pour GNV, l’efficacité énergétique est un levier stratégique, et pas seulement un objectif environnemental : elle influe sur la compétitivité, sur la qualité du service et sur la capacité à accélérer la transition du transport maritime. L’obtention de cette certification confirme la solidité d’une démarche que nous construisons avec cohérence, à travers un plan d’investissements sans précédent pour le renouvellement de la flotte, la modernisation des navires existants et le renforcement de nos systèmes de management. Nous croyons que la durabilité se mesure à la capacité de traduire les engagements en processus, technologies et résultats concrets, et cette reconnaissance nous encourage à poursuivre avec détermination dans cette voie, avec le Groupe MSC et toutes les personnes qui travaillent chaque jour à bord et à terre », a déclaré Matteo Catani, Directeur général de GNV . « La certification ISO 50001 représente un résultat de grande valeur pour GNV, non seulement par l’ampleur et la complexité du périmètre certifié, mais surtout parce qu’elle reconnaît une démarche concrète et structurée vers une gestion de l’énergie toujours plus efficace. GNV démontre comment durabilité, innovation et efficacité peuvent être intégrées dans la stratégie et les activités quotidiennes d’un grand opérateur du transport maritime. En tant que LRQA, nous sommes fiers d’accompagner GNV dans cette démarche et je tiens à adresser mes félicitations au management et à toutes les personnes qui ont contribué à ce jalon important » , a déclaré Vincenzo Amato, General Manager de LRQA Italy . « La certification ISO 50001 nous permet de consolider et de rendre encore plus systématique le travail sur la gestion de l’énergie, à travers le suivi des consommations, l’analyse des performances et l’identification d’opportunités d’amélioration. Cette démarche est rendue possible par l’engagement du département dédié à l’efficacité énergétique, en étroite collaboration avec le personnel de bord et les autres parties prenantes. Le système concerne non seulement les navires, mais aussi les structures et les processus de l’entreprise, en favorisant une plus grande attention à l’utilisation des ressources énergétiques. La certification représente un pas supplémentaire et un encouragement à poursuivre les actions d’efficacité, en valorisant les compétences internes et les solutions technologiques disponibles » , a commenté Ivana Melillo, Energy Efficiency Director de GNV . The post GNV obtient la certification ISO 50001 pour son système de management de l’énergie appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Crack the whip on narcotics trafficking and restore Ghana’s image – Ntim Fordjour to Mahama
items.description: The Ranking Member on Parliament’s Defence and Interior Committee, Rev. John Ntim Fordjour, has challenged President John Dramani Mahama to take decisive action against narcotics trafficking, warning that repeated cocaine seizures involving shipments linked to Ghana are damaging the country’s international reputation. In a post on X on Thursday, November 12, the lawmaker questioned the status of investigations the President ordered into the alleged Gran Canaria cocaine flights, and demanded an update on the government’s commitment to a zero-tolerance approach to drug trafficking. Mr President @JDMahama How far with the investigation you ordered into the Gran Canaria cocaine flights? What happened to your commitment of ensuring zero tolerance to drug trafficking? Ghana under your tenure now faces international embarrassment as ranked 5th in the world in cocaine trafficking to Belgium. Since your X post on 1st April 2025, almost every month records major drug busts running into tons and hundreds of millions of dollars, busted overseas, linked to Ghana. Under your tenure, over $3bn worth of drugs have been busted overseas linked to Ghana with several billions trafficked undetected. Ghana’s once reputed image keeps sinking by the day. Govt officials, drug networks and state agencies are milking hundreds of millions from the trade under your watch and yet the enabler agreement signed by Okudzeto with Columbia for direct and open shipments between Tema and Cartegena Ports has not been cancelled. Your Excellency, this is certainly not the reset legacy Ghanaians hoped for at your second coming. Crack the whip and restore Ghana’s sinking image to the once reputable narcotics-intolerable state. — John Ntim Fordjour MP (@NtimFordjour) November 12, 2026 He cited recent drug interceptions overseas, including the seizure of 2,600 kilogrammes of cocaine concealed in a shipment of coconuts from Ghana at Spain’s Port of Valencia, and the confiscation of nearly 3.9 tonnes of cocaine from a Ghana-origin container at France’s Port of Dunkirk in September. Rev. Ntim Fordjour claimed that more than US$3 billion worth of drugs linked to Ghana had been seized overseas under the current administration, with other consignments allegedly passing undetected. He also referenced a reported ranking that places Ghana fifth globally in cocaine trafficking to Belgium. The lawmaker further questioned why an agreement he said was signed by Okudzeto with Colombia to facilitate direct shipments between the ports of Tema and Cartagena had not been cancelled. He also alleged that state officials and agencies were benefiting from the drug trade, although he provided no evidence in the post to substantiate the claims. The Assin South MP urged President Mahama to act against those involved in the trade and take steps to restore Ghana’s reputation as a country intolerant of narcotics trafficking. The latest Spanish interception led to the arrest of two people in Almeria after cocaine was discovered hidden beneath false compartments in wooden boxes used to transport coconuts. Spanish authorities have not identified any Ghanaian nationals as suspects or announced arrests in Ghana.

items.title: Une femme de culture engagée pour les droits des artistes africains
items.description: À travers Kumbati Records, Kumbati-Podcast et son engagement au sein de la Fondation SACAME (Sayon Camara Mères et Enfants), Saran Cissoko entend contribuer à une meilleure structuration de l’industrie musicale africaine. Entre défense des droits d’auteur, accompagnement des artistes et action humanitaire, cette professionnelle de la culture fait de la valorisation du patrimoine musical africain son principal cheval de bataille. La question des droits d’auteur reste un défi majeur dans l’industrie musicale africaine.Alors que les œuvres circulent désormais au-delà des frontières grâce aux plateformes numériques, de nombreux artistes peinent encore à maîtriser les mécanismes de protection, de gestion et de rémunération de leurs créations. C’est sur ce terrain que s’est engagée Saran Cissoko, femme de culture, consultante en direction artistique et spécialiste de la gestion des droits et revenus des artistes. Lire aussi: Artistes en précarité : quelle traçabilité pour leurs revenus ? Fille de la chanteuse guinéenne Sayon Camara, elle a grandi dans un environnement où la musique occupe une place centrale. Mais au-delà de cet héritage familial, c’est une expérience personnelle qui a progressivement orienté son engagement professionnel : la nécessité de retrouver, de préserver et de valoriser le patrimoine musical de sa mère, constitué de douze albums. Une démarche qui lui permet de mesurer les difficultés auxquelles sont confrontés les artistes dans la gestion de leurs œuvres et la préservation de leur héritage artistique.De cette expérience découle une conviction : le talent ne suffit pas toujours à garantir une carrière durable. Encore faut-il disposer des outils et des connaissances nécessaires pour protéger ses créations et en tirer des revenus. Kumbati-Podcast, un outil de sensibilisation C'est dans cette dynamique que s'inscrit Kumbati Records, dont Saran Cissoko est la présidente-directrice générale. À travers cette structure de production et d'accompagnement artistique, elle entend participer à la professionnalisation de l'écosystème musical africain et offrir aux créateurs des perspectives de valorisation de leur travail. Parmi ses initiatives figure Kumbati-Podcast, une nouvelle rubrique consacrée aux droits d'auteur et à la propriété intellectuelle. L'objectif est de rendre ces questions plus accessibles aux artistes et aux professionnels de la culture, souvent confrontés à des difficultés dans la compréhension de leurs droits. « Kumbati-Podcast est désormais votre nouvelle rubrique qui vous permet de découvrir, de connaître vos droits et le fruit de votre travail », annonce la plateforme dans sa présentation. À travers ce programme, Saran Cissoko veut ouvrir un espace d'échange et de sensibilisation autour de problématiques essentielles : la protection des œuvres, la gestion des droits et la juste rémunération des créateurs. Une manière de rappeler que derrière chaque chanson, chaque composition et chaque création se trouvent du travail, du talent et des investissements qui méritent reconnaissance. SACAME, l'autre dimension de son engagement Son implication ne se limite toutefois pas au secteur musical. Saran Cissoko est également associée aux activités de la Fondation SACAME (Sayon Camara Mères et Enfants), une initiative humanitaire portée par la chanteuse guinéenne Sayon Camara. La fondation inscrit son action dans une dynamique de solidarité en faveur des mères et des enfants. Cet engagement social vient compléter son investissement dans le domaine culturel. Il traduit une volonté de faire de son parcours un espace d'action dépassant les seules questions de production et de carrière artistique. Entre héritage familial, entrepreneuriat culturel et engagement humanitaire, Saran Cissoko construit ainsi un parcours à la croisée de plusieurs univers. Son ambition est de contribuer à un environnement dans lequel les artistes africains ne seraient plus seulement reconnus pour leurs performances, mais également pour la valeur économique et patrimoniale de leurs créations. A.N

items.title: Oyo targets $3.4trn African market for artisans, creative businesses
items.description: By Adeola Badru Oyo State Government has unveiled plans to position local artisans, creative entrepreneurs and small businesses to tap into the estimated $3.4 trillion African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) market and expand their access to global export opportunities. The state government said it was determined to transform its rich cultural heritage into a commercially viable creative industry capable of generating wealth, creating employment and attracting foreign exchange through exports. Governor Seyi Makinde stated this at the Investment and Export Promotion for Art and Craft Businesses in Oyo State, tagged Oyo State Business Forum 2026: Where Oyo’s Makers Meet the World’s Buyers. The forum, held at the Ministry of Local Government Hall, Secretariat, Ibadan, was organised by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism in collaboration with the Oyo State Investment Promotion Agency (OYSIPA). Represented by the Secretary to the State Government, Prof. Musibau Babatunde, the governor said the initiative was a deliberate effort to reposition Oyo State as a major destination for creative enterprise and investment. Addressing government officials, investors, development partners, captains of industry and entrepreneurs, Makinde said the state was determined to ensure that locally produced goods gained international recognition and commercial value. “Today, we are not just gathered for another forum. We are gathered to make a declaration that Oyo State will no longer be known for its history, but for its entrepreneurial spirit. “We are gathered here around a common ambition to transform what our people create with their hands into products that the world recognises, values and buys,” he said. Tracing Oyo’s commercial heritage to the old Oyo Empire, Babatunde noted that the state had historically played an important role in regional commerce, with its people trading textiles, beads, ironworks and other products across West Africa long before the emergence of modern international trade. He said AfCFTA had presented another significant opportunity for the state to reclaim its position as a commercial powerhouse by expanding the reach of locally manufactured and processed products. According to him, the continental trade agreement is creating a single African market of approximately 1.4 billion people, with a combined economic output of about $3.4 trillion. He, however, challenged the state to move beyond recognising the opportunities offered by the agreement and take concrete steps to secure a significant share of its benefits. “The question before us is simple. Will Oyo State merely absorb this opportunity, or will we position ourselves to benefit from it? My answer is clear. Oyo State will be an active participant, and our artisans, creative entrepreneurs and small businesses will be among the driving forces of this ambition,” he said. The SSG further claimed that Oyo State was the first sub-national government in Africa to key into the AfCFTA framework, adding that the state was already positioning itself to participate meaningfully in continental trade. Speaking directly to artisans and producers across the state, including those in Oyo town, Ibadan and other communities, Babatunde said their skills and products possessed enormous economic potential that remained largely untapped. He cited wood carvers in Oyo town, women producing Adire fabrics in Ibadan and other traditional craftsmen whose skills had been passed down through generations as examples of creative resources that could be transformed into globally competitive businesses. He lamented that many local producers continued to receive recognition for their creativity without enjoying commensurate financial rewards, as much of the commercial value generated along the supply chain was captured by other players. “For too long, our artisans have received recognition for their creativity without necessarily receiving the financial rewards that their efforts deserve. “In many instances, producers remain confined to small-scale operations while greater commercial value is captured further along the supply chain. That situation must change,” he said. Babatunde urged artisans to see themselves as entrepreneurs operating within a viable industry rather than merely small-scale producers, noting that their products could compete as distinctive cultural and luxury goods in international markets. He said local producers needed access to capital, improved production facilities, modern technology, organised markets and business support to maximise their potential. “What we need is not sympathy. We need access to capital, better production facilities, modern technology, organised markets and the right business support. And that is precisely the kind of opportunity we want this forum to create,” he added. Highlighting the prospects of Nigeria’s non-oil export sector, the SSG cited figures attributed to the Nigeria Export Promotion Council indicating that the country’s non-oil exports reached a record $6.1 billion in 2025, compared with $5.46 billion in 2020. He also disclosed that export volumes rose to 8.02 million metric tonnes, describing the performance as evidence of the growing contribution of non-oil exports to economic diversification. He said Oyo State must position its businesses to benefit from the expanding international market by strengthening production capacity and improving the quality of exportable products. However, he noted that identifying products with export potential was only the first step, stressing that local businesses must be equipped to meet international standards on quality, packaging, consistency, pricing and delivery. He also emphasised the need for producers to understand rules of origin, certification procedures and other trade requirements under AfCFTA to enable them to access African markets without unnecessary difficulties. “Our ambition should be to move from simply producing goods for local consumption to developing competitive businesses capable of serving customers across Africa, Europe, Asia and the Americas,” he said. Addressing investors and private-sector representatives, Babatunde declared that Oyo State was open for business, urging them to invest not only in locally made products but also in the production systems, infrastructure and business environment required to make them globally competitive. He identified production clusters, export infrastructure and human capital development as three critical areas requiring investment. On the government’s role, the SSG said the state recognised that the opportunities could not be realised through private investment alone, noting that government must provide an enabling environment for businesses to thrive. He said the administration was improving the investment climate through its investment promotion framework and the Oyo State Non-Stop Investment Centre to simplify investor engagement, strengthen coordination among government institutions and reduce administrative bottlenecks. He also listed infrastructure development, including the Bada Sakura Road Rehabilitation Project and initiatives around the Badena Dry Ponds, as part of efforts to improve connectivity, facilitate the movement of goods and strengthen the state’s economic competitiveness. Babatunde further disclosed that the government was strengthening support for artisans and small businesses through cooperative structures and enterprise development initiatives, particularly in business registration, financial services, credit facilities and other forms of enterprise support. Illustrating the global potential of Oyo’s indigenous products, he envisioned Adire fabrics produced in Ibadan finding ready markets in New York and London, while leather products, wood carvings, sculptures and beadworks became recognised brands in international retail outlets, exhibitions and cultural markets. “Imagine a future where the next Ashrafi displayed on the fashion runway in Paris proudly carries the label, ‘Made in Iseyin Oyo State, Nigeria’. “Imagine Adire produced in Ibadan bought by customers in New York, London and other international markets,” he said. He described the vision as achievable through deliberate investment, improved production capacity, innovation and effective partnerships. Babatunde consequently invited investors to explore opportunities in the state’s creative industries, while urging diplomatic partners to support market access, trade facilitation and international business connections for local enterprises. He also charged artisans to embrace innovation, improve production standards and position their businesses to take advantage of emerging opportunities. The SSG said cultural heritage should be regarded not merely as something to preserve but also as an economic resource capable of generating prosperity for present and future generations. In his remarks, the Commissioner for Culture and Tourism, Dr. Wasiu Olatunbosun, urged artisans, business owners and creative entrepreneurs to take responsibility for promoting their products and services through digital marketing and e-commerce platforms. He said digital technology had made it possible for businesses operating in local communities to showcase their products to international audiences without necessarily establishing physical outlets abroad. “It is going to be a joint thing, but you start it from your end. You that is the creator or the owner of the business, you must also make sure that you sell yourself, your product, your commodity and your services to the whole world. “And the best way you can reach the whole world is through social marketing or e-commerce,” he said. Olatunbosun described the internet as a global marketplace where entrepreneurs could showcase their products, interact with prospective customers and receive feedback to improve their businesses. He urged producers to package their goods professionally and maximise digital platforms to attract buyers and establish lasting business relationships. He also said the state government was working to create opportunities for investors to discover indigenous products and establish direct relationships with local producers. The commissioner encouraged local businesses to participate in domestic and international exhibitions, describing such platforms as opportunities to display their products, attract investors, establish commercial relationships and improve their visibility. The forum brought together stakeholders from the public and private sectors, entrepreneurs, artisans and development partners to explore investment opportunities, strengthen export capacity and establish business connections to take Oyo State’s indigenous products to international markets. The post Oyo targets $3.4trn African market for artisans, creative businesses appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: COP31 : au Mali, les retombées des conférences sur le climat restent peu perceptibles pour les paysans
items.description: Le Premier ministre malien General Abdoulaye Maïga est arrive ce mercredi a Antalya, en Türkiye pour participer a la 31 e Conference sur le climat COP. Au Mali, la question des retombees concretes de ces rencontres internationales sur les populations rurales reste posee. Malgre les engagements pris pour soutenir l'adaptation au changement climatique, de nombreux producteurs affirment ne pas en ressentir les effets sur le terrain. Entre manque d'information, acces limite aux financements et insuffisance de l'accompagnement, les attentes des paysans restent importantes. a Sikasso, region consideree comme l'un des principaux bassins agricoles du Mali, Abdramane Bamba, cultivateur, dit connaître tres peu les conferences internationales sur le climat et leurs eventuelles retombees. Pour lui, les annonces faites a l'occasion de ces rencontres ne se traduisent pas necessairement par une amelioration des conditions de travail des producteurs. « Bien que l'on affirme que cette pratique est avantageuse pour les agriculteurs, je dois temoigner que nous n'en ressentons pas les effets. Il est possible que d'autres producteurs en tirent profit, mais ce n'est malheureusement pas notre cas », deplore-t-il. Le cultivateur estime que les producteurs ont davantage besoin d'un accompagnement direct que de simples annonces. S'il avait l'occasion de participer a une COP, il plaiderait notamment pour un renforcement de la formation et un meilleur acces aux intrants agricoles. « Nous voyons de grandes annonces a la television tous les jours, mais cela reste tres loin de notre realite et personne ne prend le temps de nous les expliquer », regrette Abdramane Bamba. Des financements climatiques qui profitent peu aux petits producteurs Ce constat est egalement releve par Dr Fode Diallo, professeur a l'Institut polytechnique rural de formation et de recherche appliquee (IPR-IFRA) de Katibougou. Selon lui, les petits producteurs, particulierement ceux vivant dans les villages, beneficient rarement de maniere directe des retombees economiques des differentes conferences sur le climat. Pour le specialiste, malgre la place accordee a l'agriculture dans les engagements climatiques, les financements annonces ne sont pas toujours entierement mobilises. « Les bailleurs de fonds promettent des financements, mais de COP en COP, vous allez constater qu'au maximum 50 % sont souvent debloques. Ce dont les producteurs beneficient, c'est peut-etre des pratiques vulgarisees et disseminees par des projets et programmes », explique-t-il. Mieux informer et impliquer les communautes rurales Face a cette situation, Dr Fode Diallo insiste sur la necessite de renforcer la communication autour des decisions prises lors des differentes COP. Il preconise egalement une implication plus importante des communautes rurales dans les rencontres internationales et les processus de prise de decision. Pour lui, les engagements climatiques ne peuvent produire pleinement leurs effets sans une meilleure prise en compte des realites des populations directement confrontees aux consequences du dereglement climatique. Lire aussi : COP31 : le Mali ambitionne de reduire ses emissions de 25,22 % d'ici 2035 L’article COP31 : au Mali, les retombées des conférences sur le climat restent peu perceptibles pour les paysans est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Mississippi’s First Black Senator in 150 Years
items.description: One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white former Democratic congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote. An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron. Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old. This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state. Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi. In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it. When the Black reporter Simeon Booker arrived in 1955 to cover the lynching of Emmett Till for Jet magazine, he wrote that he witnessed “not only raw hatred, but state condoned terror.” This apparatus of state-condoned terror was still active into the 1960s. As Thomas Ricks writes in Waging a Good War , his history of the civil-rights movement as a nonviolent military campaign, when the legendary civil-rights organizer Bob Moses went down to Mississippi he was “assaulted and jailed repeatedly, sometimes simply for speaking to white people as equals.” In 1963, Moses and other organizers survived a drive-by shooting. He later wrote to the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee that Mississippi was extremely dangerous—“we were just like sitting ducks” and “people were just going to be wiped out.” [ Adam Serwer: Even where MAGA won, MAGA lost ] The point of all this terror was to prevent what happened yesterday, when Democrat Scott Colom defeated Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. Hyde-Smith had attended a segregation academy as a child—private schools set up in the South to circumvent the Brown v. Board of Education ruling to integrate public schools. She had previously blocked Colom’s appointment to the federal bench . On Election Night, Hyde-Smith had declared victory , saying, “I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being a U.S. Senator.” That was a little premature. “In Mississippi, our prayers often change the course of history,” Colom said in his victory speech last night.“It’s not something that I did, y’all. It’s something that we did. All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this.” The last Black man to have served as a U.S. senator from Mississippi, Blanche Bruce—back then senators were appointed by the state legislature—was born enslaved in 1841. His mother was enslaved, and his father was her master in the eyes of the law. One of Bruce’s votes was against the Republican-supported Chinese Exclusion Act, which he explained as a vote of conscience and solidarity, “representing as I do a people who are considered essentially disqualified from the privileges and immunities of American citizenship.” Before the turn of the 20th century, Mississippi was majority-Black. State-tolerated (or state-encouraged) terror led many Black Mississippians to flee north during the Great Migration. Today, Mississippi still has the highest proportion of Black residents of any state. Before the Voting Rights Act was passed in 1965, law and violence kept Black Mississippians disenfranchised; after, racially polarized voting would place a hard ceiling on the aspirations of every Black candidate in this red state. The last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate was John Stennis, an avowed segregationist who, as a prosecutor in the 1930s, had led the prosecution of three Black men who had been tortured into confessions, a case that led the Supreme Court to rule in 1936 that such confessions are inadmissible under the Fourteenth Amendment. This is all to say, as one famous Mississippian put it, that “the past is never dead. It’s not even past.” Mississippi today is not the Mississippi of Dark Journey , but we are living in a world inextricably shaped by it. Multiracial democracy in America is young; it emerged only in the lifetimes of the people who are still currently governing the country. It is younger than the president. It is younger than most of the justices on the Supreme Court. And it has been under assault. The past decade has seen a relentless attack on its foundations from people who remember the time before multiracial democracy as a golden age. It was not a golden age in Mississippi, not for people like Herbert Lee, or Bob Moses, or Fannie Lou Hamer. Conservatives have undone or undermined many of the laws and constitutional amendments passed to ensure that Black Americans could exercise their rights as full citizens. The Supreme Court has slowly chipped away at the Voting Rights Act, most recently ruling in Louisiana v. Callais that racist voting restrictions are constitutional if they are passed with partisan, rather than racist, intent. This standard would permit many Jim Crow–era laws that were superficially race-neutral but racist in intent. As McMillen observed, in pre-1965 Mississippi, “much of the exclusionary process was necessarily left to the discriminatory application of otherwise racially neutral law.” (If lawmakers want to disenfranchise Democratic voters, and those voters just happen to be Black—by coincidence, of course!—that’s fine.) Many Republican-controlled states in the South responded to the ruling by gerrymandering Black-majority districts out of existence. At the time, the former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale gleefully speculated that “if states are aggressive, we could see a healthy majority in the House perpetually.” Republicans might never have to worry about courting Black voters again. Black Americans responded to this assault on the foundations of their freedom with terrific fervor in the midterms. Black-voter turnout in the South appears to have surged last week to a hair below levels usually seen when presidents are on the ballot. That, along with increased white support for Democrats, helped put previously deep-red states like Mississippi into contention. [ Adam Serwer: Texas Republicans get washed ] The next Congress will have seven Black U.S. senators including Colom, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Tim Scott of South Carolina, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Cory Booker of New Jersey—the most ever in history. There will be five contemporaneous Black governors in the United States in 2027, with Wes Moore in Maryland, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Byron Donalds in Florida, David Crowley in Wisconsin, and Aaron Ford in Nevada. Before this election, there had been only three such elected governors: Moore, Douglas Wilder from Virginia, and Deval Patrick of Massachusetts. The first Black governor of any state, P. B. S. Pinchback of Louisiana, who inherited the office in 1872 after his running mate was impeached, required the intervention of the Grant administration to prevent a white-supremacist uprising in Louisiana. He was in office for 39 days. There would not be another Black governor in America for more than a century. The fact that Black voters defeated efforts to limit their political power does not make such efforts morally acceptable or justifiable, of course. As Jamelle Bouie wrote in The New York Times this week, “That Americans of all stripes can overcome obstacles to voting does not mean that they should have to. And high Black turnout does not obviate the need for legislation to secure the right to vote.” Bruce would be proud of Colom, I think, albeit initially confused as to why he was running as a Democrat. It took a century from Reconstruction to the civil-rights movement to restore the rights of Black voters, and far less time before politicians and justices began to curtail them again. Yet the project of snuffing out Black aspirations to equal citizenship will always fail. It failed in 1875. It failed in 1965. And it failed in 2026, with Callais . It will always fail, even if it takes a hundred years. Or a hundred and fifty.

items.title: Nigerian man shot dead by Malaysian police after machete attack on officer
items.description: A Nigerian man identified as Chibuzo has been shot dead by Malaysian police after allegedly attacking an officer with a machete and severing his wrist. The incident occurred on Wednesday, November 11, at a residential property in Desa Aman Puri, Kepong, according to local authorities. A video circulating online showed the suspect wielding a machete and attacking police officers, leaving one of the personnel with his right wrist severed while attempting to defend himself. Malaysia’s Police Chief, Datuk Shazeli Kahar, said the injured officer was rushed to a hospital, where he is receiving treatment and undergoing surgery in an attempt to reattach his severed hand. Kahar explained that officers opened fire on the Nigerian after he attacked them with the machete while they were attempting to arrest him. He said the police had earlier received a complaint from a member of the public about a man who was allegedly in an unstable mental state and behaving aggressively. Following the report, a team comprising police officers, personnel of the Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department (JBPM) and officials of the Health Ministry (MOH) was dispatched to the scene to manage the situation. The officers subsequently attempted to apprehend the suspect, leading to the violent confrontation that resulted in his death. The post Nigerian man shot dead by Malaysian police after machete attack on officer appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: West Africa, a new hub of global cocaine trafficking – Report
items.description: Dozens of cocaine packages piled up, weighing in at four tonnes and valued at $317 million — the seizure by Liberian police in July was a stark symbol of west Africa’s expanding role in the global cocaine trade. In recent years, the region has become a favoured route for traffickers moving drugs from producing countries in South America to Europe, where the highly lucrative cocaine market has exploded. Drug trafficking is now “one of the greatest threats” facing Liberia, President Joseph Boakai said in a national address in August, after several large-scale seizures. “Drugs are destroying young lives, weakening families, fuelling violence,” he warned. Politics has been tarnished too. Following the major drugs busts, former Liberian vice president Jewel Howard-Taylor was arrested for alleged involvement in an international drug trafficking network. But Liberia is by no means unique — the drugs trafficking scourge is region-wide. – Regional scourge – In neighbouring Sierra Leone, one of Europe’s most wanted cocaine traffickers, the convicted fugitive Dutchman Jos Leijdekkers, is operating with apparent support from the highest echelons of power, according to law enforcement, local testimonies and court documents gathered by AFP. “All the states in west Africa are vulnerable to cocaine trafficking,” Lucia Bird, west Africa director at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), told AFP. “The region is perfectly positioned between the cultivation areas in Latin America and consumption markets, particularly in Europe,” she said. A GI-TOC report published in March spotlighted the issue. Around 30 percent of the drug consumed in 2025 in Europe went through west Africa, according to estimates in the report. But the true scale of the trafficking remains unknown — it is difficult to quantify given its illegal nature and the analysis of seizures is not a reliable indicator. – Maritime route – Several factors have contributed in recent years to the growing importance of the west Africa route, which is largely maritime. With improvements to its port infrastructure and road networks, west Africa has become more attractive to traffickers and its ports increasingly well-connected hubs. Although transporting drugs via the region takes longer and is more expensive, “the risk of having your product seized is lower”, Bird told AFP. As Europe has tightened its controls on ships coming from South America, cargoes originating in west Africa attract less scrutiny from European customs. But with west Africa increasingly seen as high-risk, Bird said perceptions and security measures were starting to change. – Overspill – As in other regions, cocaine trafficking fuels corruption among local elites and political decision-makers. This has “profound implications for governance and devastating effects on the provision of public services and the socio-economic development of states”, the GI-TOC report said. Another problem is the overspill from the trade in bulk onto the domestic market. Smaller dealers and traffickers are sometimes paid in kind — namely, in cocaine — but lacking sufficient channels to resell it in Europe, the white powder is dumped on the local market and sold at affordable prices. This has led to “an increase in the consumption of powdered cocaine — and, to a much greater extent, crack — over the past five years,” according to the report. Three countries stand out for the particularly low price of cocaine on the local market: Guinea-Bissau, Sierra Leone and Mali. items.title: Adu-Boahene acquitted on two counts as court orders him and his wife to open their defence
items.description: The Accra High Court has given former National Signals Bureau (NSB) Director-General Kwabena Adu-Boahene and his wife, Angela Adjei-Boateng, three weeks to file witness statements if they wish to testify in their defence in the GH¢49.1 million cyber-defence case. The statements are to be filed on or before December 4, 2026. The court also ordered the accused persons to open their defences on the remaining charges, while acquitting and discharging Adu-Boahene on two counts after the defence filed a no-case-to-answer submission. The case has been adjourned to December 10, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. for continuation. Mr Adu-Boahene, his wife and their company, Advantage Solutions Limited, were facing 11 charges, including stealing, conspiracy to steal, causing financial loss to the state, using public office for profit and money laundering. They have pleaded not guilty to all the charges. The prosecution alleged that the accused persons dishonestly diverted GH¢49.1 million intended for the procurement of a US$7 million cyber-defence system, with only US$1.75 million paid to the Israeli supplier, ISC Holdings. The defence, led by Samuel Atta Akyea, argued in its submission of no case that the prosecution had failed to establish that the GH¢49.1 million was public property, that the transactions were unauthorised or that the accused persons acted with criminal intent. The lawyers also questioned the prosecution’s failure to call key witnesses, including the late National Security Coordinator, Joshua Kyeremeh, who signed the disputed cheques. The prosecution called four witnesses before closing its case. The accused persons have until December 4 to file their witness statements, should they wish to do so. The trial is scheduled to resume on December 10 at 9:30 a.m., when proceedings are expected to continue with the defence stage.

items.title: Full list of Man United managers sacked since Sir Alex Ferguson’s exit
items.description: Man United have parted ways with seven permanent managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013, following the dismissal of Michael Carrick on Thursday. Carrick became the latest casualty of the club’s managerial instability after United endured a disappointing start to the 2026/27 Premier League season, leaving them in the relegation zone. The former Man United midfielder was appointed head coach in January 2026, initially on an interim basis, before being handed a permanent contract in May after guiding the club to a third-place finish and Champions League qualification. However, a poor run of results, including just three victories in 15 matches across all competitions this season, ultimately ended his 10-month spell at Old Trafford. His departure means seven permanent managers have now left the club since Ferguson brought his remarkable 26-year reign to an end in 2013. Here is the full list of Man United managers who have been sacked since Ferguson’s departure. 1. David Moyes (2013–2014) David Moyes was appointed as Ferguson’s successor in June 2013 on a six-year contract, having impressed during his time at Everton. However, the Scottish manager struggled to maintain United’s dominance, with the club enduring a disappointing campaign that saw them miss out on Champions League qualification for the first time since 1995. Moyes was dismissed on April 22, 2014, after just 10 months in charge. 2. Louis van Gaal (2014–2016) Former Netherlands manager Louis van Gaal succeeded Moyes in May 2014, bringing considerable experience and an impressive managerial pedigree to Old Trafford. He guided United to Champions League qualification in his first season and won the FA Cup in 2016. However, the club’s failure to qualify for the Champions League, despite winning the FA Cup, led to his dismissal on May 23, 2016, just two days after lifting the trophy. 3. Jose Mourinho (2016–2018) Jose Mourinho became United’s third permanent manager after Ferguson in May 2016. The Portuguese won three trophies during his first season, including the Europa League and League Cup, before finishing second in the Premier League in the 2017/18 campaign. However, tensions within the club, disagreements over transfers and a poor start to the 2018/19 season led to his dismissal on December 18, 2018. 4. Ole Gunnar Solskjaer (2018–2021) Former United striker Ole Gunnar Solskjaer initially joined the club as caretaker manager in December 2018 following Mourinho’s departure. His impressive start earned him the permanent position, and he guided United to a second-place Premier League finish in the 2020/21 season. However, a series of disappointing results, including a humiliating 5-0 home defeat to Liverpool, increased pressure on the Norwegian. He was eventually dismissed on November 21, 2021, following a 4-1 defeat to Watford. 5. Erik ten Hag (2022–2024) Erik ten Hag took charge of Manchester United in 2022 after establishing himself as one of Europe’s promising coaches during his time at Ajax. The Dutchman won the League Cup in his first season and followed it with an FA Cup triumph in 2024. However, inconsistent performances and United’s poor start to the 2024/25 campaign led to his dismissal on October 28, 2024, following a 2-1 defeat to West Ham United. 6. Ruben Amorim (2024–2026) Ruben Amorim was appointed in November 2024 after impressing at Sporting Lisbon, where he won domestic honours and established an attacking style of football. However, his time at Old Trafford was largely disappointing, with United struggling for consistency and failing to establish themselves among the Premier League’s leading sides. The Portuguese won just 24 of his 63 matches in charge, recording a 38.1 per cent win rate. He was dismissed on January 5, 2026, after 14 months in charge. 7. Michael Carrick (2026) Michael Carrick became the seventh permanent manager to leave Manchester United since Ferguson’s retirement. Appointed in January 2026, Carrick initially enjoyed an impressive spell, guiding United to third place in the Premier League and securing Champions League qualification. His performances earned him a two-year contract in May 2026. However, United’s fortunes deteriorated in the 2026/27 season, with the club recording just three wins in 15 matches across all competitions. The disappointing run left the Red Devils in the Premier League relegation zone, prompting the club to dismiss him on November 12, 2026. Carrick’s departure has further extended United’s search for stability in the dugout, with the club still struggling to replicate the success enjoyed under Ferguson. items.title: El-Rufai supporters, ex-ADC aspirants defect to APC in Kaduna
items.description: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo Hundreds of supporters of former Kaduna State Governor, Nasir El-Rufai, including members of the El-Rufai Boys Vanguard, Nasiriyya Youth Movement, former African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidates and party executives, have defected to the All Progressives Congress (APC), pledging support for Governor Uba Sani. The defectors, led by Hon. Ibrahim Khalil Dan Kasa, a former ADC House of Assembly candidate for Unguwan Sanusi Constituency, announced their decision on Thursday at the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ) Press Centre, Kaduna. Dan Kasa said the decision followed extensive consultations across the three senatorial districts of the state, adding that the group had withdrawn its support for the ADC governorship candidate, Isa Ashiru Kudan. He claimed that the defection involved more than 2,000 ward coordinators, former candidates, aspirants, youth mobilisers and party executives across Kaduna State. The defectors attributed their decision to alleged internal divisions, marginalisation, denial of party tickets to their preferred aspirants and what they described as the absence of a clear policy direction within the ADC. They also accused the party of neglecting women and youths who, according to them, were initially promised opportunities and active participation in its political activities. Dan Kasa further alleged that the leadership of the El-Rufai Youth Movement failed to protect members from what he described as mistreatment and neglect within the party. He said the group became particularly dissatisfied with the ADC’s candidate selection process, citing the alleged refusal to consider candidates recommended by El-Rufai for the Kawo and Doka Gabasawa State Assembly constituencies. According to him, despite supporting Ashiru’s political campaign for seven months, the group had yet to see a clearly articulated manifesto or policy blueprint outlining his plans for Kaduna State. He also accused some members of Ashiru’s campaign team of disparaging El-Rufai’s political legacy despite relying on his supporters for grassroots mobilisation and campaign activities. The former ADC candidate said ward coordinators and grassroots mobilisers were equally abandoned without adequate logistical, security and welfare support. Explaining their decision to align with Governor Sani, Dan Kasa said the governor had demonstrated commitment to continuity, infrastructural development, rural transformation and inclusive governance. He particularly commended Sani for completing more than 80 per cent of critical urban and infrastructure projects initiated by the previous administration. The group also praised the governor’s efforts to promote religious and ethnic harmony, develop rural communities and provide opportunities for young people to participate in governance. “Politics without tangible governance is meaningless noise,” Dan Kasa said, arguing that the Sani administration had demonstrated greater commitment to development and political inclusiveness. He, however, maintained that their respect for El-Rufai remained intact, stressing that personal loyalty should not prevent them from making political decisions they considered beneficial to Kaduna State. The defectors subsequently announced the dissolution of their political support structures within the ADC and their integration into the APC. They also pledged to deploy their grassroots mobilisation and media structures in support of Governor Sani’s administration and what they described as the continued progress and stability of Kaduna State. items.title: Rawlings’ family, NDC mark 6th anniversary of his death with wreath-laying ceremony
items.description: A wreath-laying ceremony has been held at the Military Cemetery in Accra to mark the sixth anniversary of the death of former President Flight Lieutenant Jerry John Rawlings. The ceremony took place on Thursday, November 12, 2026, with members of his family, representatives of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) and senior military officers paying tribute to his memory. His daughter, Yaa Asantewaa Rawlings, laid the first wreath on behalf of the former President’s children. Colonel Joshua Agbotui (Rtd) followed with a wreath on behalf of the Agbotui and allied families, while the NDC General Secretary, Fifi Fiavi Kwetey, laid the final wreath on behalf of the party in recognition of Mr Rawlings’ service to Ghana and his place in the country’s history. Among those present were members of the former President’s family and a delegation from the NDC Headquarters. Senior military officers who attended included the Chief of Staff at the General Headquarters, Air Vice Marshal Joshua Lartei Mensah-Larkai; Deputy Chief Staff Officer in charge of Logistics, Rear Admiral Francis Ayitevi Nyarko; and Deputy Chief Staff Officer in charge of Operations and Training, Major General Glover Annan.
