«Où sont les pièges à miel ?» Dourov tacle Paris, sur fond de l’affaire Huang-Huang
items.description: « C'est injuste que les PDG qui ne sont pas attires par les filles asiatiques aient moins d'opportunites de rencontres amoureuses de la part des services de renseignement. » Dans un message poste le 11 novembre sur Telegram puis le lendemain sur X, le directeur general de Telegram, accuse de « complicite de terrorisme » en Russie, est revenu sur l'affaire qui secoue la tech mondiale… a sa maniere. « Ou sont les pieges a miel francais, russes ou iraniens ? Pas une seule espionne envoyee dans ma direction. Est-ce qu'ils essaient au moins ? », a ajoute cet informaticien a qui Emmanuel Macron avait octroye la nationalite francaise, puis interpelle par les autorites francaises a sa descente d'avion au Bourget a l'ete 2024. © Telegram / Pavel Dourov « La France est excusee », a embraye Dourov avant de conclure : « ses dirigeants ne s'interessent pas aux femmes. Quant a tous les autres : faites plus d'efforts ! ». Cette saillie survient en plein feuilleton « Huang-Huang », dont les medias internationaux font leurs choux gras depuis la revelation que le patron de Nvidia, ex-premiere capitalisation mondiale, Jensen Huang a couche avec une supposee espionne chinoise. Le NYT en rajoute une couche, Nvdia chancele Tout eclate le 29 octobre, avec la publication d'un article-fleuve du New York Times (NYT), faisant etant d'« une relation etroite » nouee entre Alice Huang, travaillant pour une entreprise de donnees basee a Singapour, et le patron taïwano-americain, cet « allie de poids du president Trump » comme le soulignait le quotidien proHillary Clinton et Kamala Harris , a quelques jours des elections de mi-mandat. Ainsi, toujours selon la meme source, qui se basait sur des « entretiens avec des personnes informees » qui « ont parle sous couvert d'anonymat », Alice Huang « transmettait directement des informations a Pekin ». « J'ai ete infidele a ma femme », avait finalement lâche Jensen Huang, sans commenter ces accusations, que Pekin a rejete, de son cote, les qualifiant de « pure invention ». « La partie americaine devrait cesser de fabriquer de tels recits d'espionnage et de s'en servir comme pretexte pour imposer un blocus technologique », a declare ce 12 novembre une porte-parole chinoise des Affaires etrangeres, Mao Ning, lors d'un point presse regulier. Depuis ces revelations de la presse americaine, la multinationale, deja malmenee sur les marches depuis debut octobre, a decroche. En l'espace d'un mois, Nvidia a perdu 23 % de sa valeur boursiere. Un plongeon accelere le 11 novembre par deux autres publications , notamment, a nouveau, du New York Times . Citant « cinq personnes ayant travaille dans l'entreprise », le quotidien assure que Jensen Huang aurait eu une autre liaison avec Kimberly Powell, vice-presidente de Nvidia en charge des soins de sante. Or, aux etats-Unis, coucher avec un collaborateur – qui plus est un subalterne – est loin d'etre une mince affaire.

items.title: UEW partners universities in Togo, Côte d’Ivoire and Benin on PhD training and research
items.description: The University of Education, Winneba (UEW), is pursuing stronger academic collaboration with three West African universities to promote joint supervision of doctoral students, research development and language proficiency programmes. The initiative involves the Université de Lomé in Togo, Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny in Côte d’Ivoire and Université d’Abomey-Calavi in Benin. The Vice-Chancellor of UEW, Professor Stephen John Mitchual, announced the development during the orientation ceremony for PhD students under the Inter-University Conference for Doctoral Studies (IUCDS) at the Université de Lomé in Togo on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. He said the partnership was expected to create opportunities for UEW doctoral students pursuing programmes in French and Ewe to undertake annual research attachments at the partner institutions to strengthen their research skills. Professor Mitchual said he hoped a final agreement would be reached among the universities to facilitate the arrangement. He also advocated joint supervision and assessment of doctoral dissertations and theses in Language and Linguistics, Literature, and Translation and Interpretation programmes. The proposed collaboration will cover PhD programmes in French, English and Ewe offered at UEW. According to the Vice-Chancellor, the three partner universities have also agreed to organise French and English language proficiency programmes for students, teaching staff and administrative personnel. He said the Université de Lomé and Université Félix Houphouët-Boigny had also proposed sending their doctoral students in English and other disciplines to UEW for English language and research skills development programmes. Professor Mitchual called for a working session between the institutions to establish the modalities for implementing the proposed arrangements. He further indicated that UEW could establish a Language Centre to develop specialised language proficiency programmes in French, English and German for students. The Vice-Chancellor said the collaboration was part of efforts to strengthen academic partnerships within the West African sub-region, improve research standards and facilitate the exchange of expertise among member institutions. The Inter-University Conference for Doctoral Studies is a collaborative platform established to promote doctoral training, interdisciplinary research, staff development and academic cooperation among participating universities. UEW hosts the permanent Executive Secretariat of the Conference through its Institute for Educational Research and Innovation Studies (IERIS).

items.title: ‘The cedi knows no political parties’ – Mahama calls for collective responsibility
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called on Ghanaians to put aside political differences and take collective responsibility for protecting the cedi, insisting that the national currency belongs to everyone and should be valued beyond party lines. He said the cedi transcended political affiliations and belonged to all Ghanaians, stressing that its value and usefulness depended on the collective confidence and trust citizens placed in the national currency. “The cedi knows no political parties. Its usefulness rests on the confidence that we Ghanaians place in it,” he said. The President made the appeal on Thursday, November 12, during the launch of the Bank of Ghana’s Heritage Series banknotes at the Bank Square in Accra. Speaking under the theme, “The Cedi, Our Future: Secure, Designed to Last,” he used the symbolism of two crocodiles joined together and sharing one stomach to illustrate why collective responsibility was important in national affairs. He said although citizens might have different political opinions and approaches to national issues, the consequences of their decisions were often shared. “That lesson of the crocodiles remains relevant in Ghana today. We may approach questions from different perspectives, but the consequences of our choices extend beyond ourselves,” he stated. Dr Mahama said the lesson was particularly relevant to the protection of the cedi, arguing that maintaining confidence in the currency required a collective commitment from citizens, regardless of their political affiliations. He also drew attention to the cultural and historical significance of the Heritage Series, explaining that the new banknotes were intended to reflect Ghana’s shared identity and the experiences that connect its people. According to him, the currency represents more than its monetary function, as the historical personalities, landmarks and cultural symbols featured on the notes also tell the story of the country. The President further described the cedi as an informal ambassador for Ghana, noting that its design could introduce the country’s history and culture to people beyond its borders. “In that sense, our currency serves as a quiet ambassador for our nation,” he said. Meanwhile, the Heritage Series introduces improvements to the physical features of Ghana’s banknotes, including enhanced security specifications designed to strengthen protection against counterfeiting. The Heritage Series is expected to circulate on December 1, alongside the existing banknotes as the central bank manages a gradual transition to the new currency.

items.title: What I Learned at a Drunk-Math Party
items.description: A t 7 o’clock on a Saturday in October, the light is dimming in Cole Valley and a group of the AI industry’s young stars is gathered on the second story of a century-old Edwardian. At first glance, it looks like any other San Francisco house party: bottles of cheap liquor on the table and awkward conversations in the living room. But there are signs that this party is different. In the kitchen sits a pile of sharp No. 2 pencils and stacks of white paper. I am drinking vodka and reviewing trigonometry. The unit circle is confusing enough as it is, but it’s even worse when you are three shots in. I am here for a “drunk deriving” party. The plan is to compete against one another in math. We are going to see who, while drunk, can score highest on a set of past problems from Oxford’s math-and-computer-science undergraduate-entrance exam. Normally this exam is taken individually, but for the party, the host sorts us into teams based on our self-professed math abilities. Asking AI researchers and start-up founders who spend their evenings at math parties to rate themselves on quantitative skill is a dicey proposition: Even those who majored in the field will report that they are bad for fear that an International Mathematical Olympiad medalist is in the room. But as a writer among mostly programmers, I figure that no one is expecting much from me. I am placed on a team with a guy who studied theoretical physics as a Rhodes Scholar. Once everyone is drunk, the host sends out the exam, a 13-page document with both multiple-choice and long-answer questions. Not only are we competing against one another; a parallel party is taking place in New York City. The winning team will be the one with the highest combined blood-alcohol levels and exam score. We have two and a half hours to complete the test, and calculators are banned. My two teammates start by tackling the multiple-choice items, a grab bag of logarithms and polynomials. I start with Question 6, a logic problem that mercifully has no numbers. It’s a Holmesian mystery about a shattered vase and four deceitful friends: Alice blames Bob, who blames Diane, who says Bob is wrong, and Charlie claims it wasn’t him. “Explain why at least one of the four must be lying,” instructs the exam. How strange , I think, to be doing math recreationally in the place where it’s all being automated . San Francisco is a city steeped in mathematics. The landscape, with its roller-coaster hills and valleys, is sinusoidal. People speak quantitatively too. At coffee shops in Pacific Heights, investors talk about scaling laws and S-curves and hockey-stick charts with exponential growth. Everything is riding on the tech industry’s improbable main bet: If machines can be taught to improve themselves ad infinitum, that will set off an age of impossible growth. The median Anthropic employee’s beliefs suggest an economy expanding by 17 percent annually by the end of the decade. Private-company valuations run into the trillions. In math, numbers can be natural, irrational, p-adic, and surreal. Here they simply feel made-up. Lately, the city’s math fixation has become literal. “What is it that mathematicians even do?” a young man across from me on the bus recently asked his friend as we heaved up Fillmore. His seatmate nodded philosophically. They were discussing AI models’ rapid progress in mathematics. At first the problems fell slowly: the unit-distance problem, the Jacobian conjecture, Navier-Stokes. Then came The Dump. In early October, OpenAI announced an internal model had obtained hundreds of mathematical results across more than a dozen subfields. A deluge of new AI-generated solutions has continued unabated ever since. Like the men on the bus, I too have recently become a bandwagon math fan. My fascination started over the summer after Jacob Tsimerman, one of this year’s Fields Medalists, warned me about the scale of the impending transformation. The day before the drunk-math party, I took the Caltrain south from San Francisco to Stanford to hang out with a pair of fifth-year math Ph.D.s who are thinking specifically about how AI is reshaping their discipline. I met with Henry Bosch, a geometer, and Shurui Liu, who works on a mysterious, constellational project called the Langlands program. The coffee shop where I met them is wedged inside Stanford’s electrical-engineering building, several hundred feet from the auditorium where, as a freshman, I took my last math exam. This put an end to a troubling 10-week course in multivariable calculus and linear algebra—the math underlying large language models—and also to my formal math studies. People study math for all kinds of reasons. Some have an aptitude for it and get high on the problem-solving. Bosch, an enthusiastic, restless man in clear-framed glasses and jeans, decided to pursue the subject in high school after his statistician father gave him a copy of Baby Rudin, an undergraduate textbook written by a Jewish Viennese exile—Walter Rudin. (Don’t be fooled by the nickname: The textbook, which is actually titled Principles of Mathematical Analysis , is famously terse.) Liu, who showed up dressed in a black Temu T-shirt printed with an esoteric computer-science joke, is as romantic as they come. When he was in elementary school, he was bad at math. He fell in love with it only after a depressive phase as a 14-year-old in northeastern China. “I could not sleep for several days. I was really worried that after I die, everything will become emptiness,” Liu recounted. His angst led him to theoretical physics, and that eventually brought him to math. Like many mathematicians, Liu delights in the subject’s purity: “Math allows you to build your own mental model of the universe,” he told me. In talking about their sadness at watching AI solve long-standing proofs, many mathematicians describe the subject as akin to art . Yet most of us grow up to develop the opposite associations. Mathematical beauty—“a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture,” as the philosopher Bertrand Russell described it—is assumed inaccessible. So while paintings and marbles are studied in crowded museum galleries, mathematical beauty is appreciated primarily by research mathematicians in their private sanctuaries. The typical math curriculum trains students to be problem solvers but fails to instill the romance that compels Liu. Now, as the machines keep improving, some mathematicians say beauty is being lost while others say a new kind of beauty is being born. They have started speaking about the crisis the way soldiers must have spoken of the French Revolution: It’s all been terribly violent or fantastically radical. “It was but a pellet of lead in a shotgun blast,” one lamented in response to an AI proof for a problem he has worked on for two decades. But Liu has kept his romantic streak. “I think AI will accelerate our understanding of the universe,” he said. When it’s supposed to rain in California, that’s all anyone talks about. The day I met Edward Frenkel was one of those days. (“Are you excited for the rain?” my curly-haired Irish neighbor asked me as I passed by him on the sidewalk.) Frenkel lives in the sloping Berkeley Hills, not far from the group houses filled with people who sincerely believe the world is about to end. This unusually depressive California weather would be apt for the apocalypse , I thought on the drive over. When I arrived, Frenkel opened the door in flip-flops and a T-shirt from a club in Ibiza. There was a DJ setup and a disco ball in his book-lined living room. The room’s windows revealed a panoramic view of the blue bay, and beyond, the endless Pacific. Had I not known Frenkel to be a world-class mathematician, I would have thought him to be a surfer. Frenkel reminded me of an older, more settled Liu. Growing up during the Cold War in the U.S.S.R., he was enchanted by quantum physics, which eventually led him to math, a subject he hadn’t cared for as a child. When he applied for entrance to Moscow’s top math program at age 16, he was denied on account of his father being Jewish. But he persisted, climbing over the university’s fence to sneak into lectures. By 21, he was a visiting professor at Harvard. Years later, he moved to Berkeley, where he has taught for three decades. Frenkel studies the Langlands program, same as Liu, a decades-long effort to connect far-flung and seemingly disparate subfields: a sort of grand unified theory of math. Alongside his research, he has made a career as a math evangelist. He wrote his 2013 book, Love and Math , to make the field’s beauty accessible to the public (“eros pervades his winsome new memoir,” one reviewer wrote at the time). Frenkel once caused a stir on campus by writing and starring in an erotic math film. One of Frenkel’s obsessions is the question of where math comes from. The objects that make up the mathematical world have bizarre properties. Consider an infinite line—we have never encountered one (the observable universe is finite) and yet we can reason together about them. The same applies to more complicated mathematical objects such as sheaves or Galois groups. Stranger yet, these mathematical objects sometimes end up describing the real world in unforeseen ways: An abstract concept first established in mathematics might become central to explaining physical phenomena decades or even centuries later. Complex numbers (which have both real and imaginary parts) were first conceived of in the 16th century but proved foundational to the development of quantum mechanics in the 1920s. So where do these mathematical objects reside? Is math something we are inventing collectively, like the Greek language, or does it exist independently of us and we are discovering it, as the Polynesians once encountered the Hawaiian Islands? (“Look, there on the horizon—a new number system!”) There is no settled answer. But Frenkel posits that mathematics is a bridge that connects our minds to reality. He has put forth a labyrinthine theory that mathematical concepts reside in the same collective unconscious proposed by the psychologist Carl Jung in the early 20th century. “I am convinced that there are deeper structures which we have not even seen yet; we cannot even imagine what they are,” Frenkel told me. This theory is desperately speculative. (“That’s a hypothesis,” he emphasized as he slurped the duck noodle soup we ordered from a nearby Thai place.) But the core idea is that mathematics is intrinsically linked to human interiority. In recent months, mathematics has proved particularly vulnerable to automation. This is partly because the field is now so expansive. Top mathematicians once made contributions across many subfields, but over the past century, the discipline has swelled such that no one has a full grasp of it. In some of AI’s most impressive work so far, the models have solved problems by connecting existing concepts: “The proof is a surprising synthesis of well-known ideas,” one mathematician explained to Quanta in describing OpenAI’s machine-generated proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. But AI’s progress in math also owes itself to the fact that math is ruthlessly objective. If a computer were to produce Swann’s Way , we could deny its genius on the grounds that it was generated by a machine. In mathematics, there’s no such room for dispute. But perhaps math does have more in common with art than is typically accepted. Matilde Marcolli, a mathematical physicist at Caltech, sees it both as a way of making sense of reality and as a form of self-expression: “Your mathematics, that is like the poem that composes itself in the mind and explodes onto the page because your life demands it,” she writes. Frenkel likes to cite William James’s declaration that science’s denial of its practitioners’ individuality would eventually look shortsighted. Perhaps it is wishful thinking to believe that the human mind remains in some ways exceptional— Never say never , the mathematicians all now solemnly hedge—but it is certainly the case that humans can do all sorts of things that machines cannot. “When we fall in love, we actually experience infinity in some sense,” Frenkel told me. Computers cannot experience heartbreak or dance the waltz. Nor, for that matter, can computers take drunk-math exams and laugh with their friends inside sweaty San Francisco apartments. “We are infinite in our capacities,” Frenkel said. When I finish the logic question, I feel delighted with my solution, not in the way of cosmic beauty, which motivates Frenkel and Liu, but a more elementary satisfaction at having completed the problem—even if a machine would have done it faster. And although I don’t much like alcohol or math, the truth is that I am having a lot of fun. Drunk deriving (this refers to the logical process used to arrive at certain mathematical results) is certainly less common than drunk driving (which, here in San Francisco, now means pregaming Modelos in a Waymo). There is strong precedent for doing math under the influence though. At a chandeliered cafe in 1930s Lviv, mathematicians including Stefan Banach, Stanisław Ulam, and John von Neumann advanced the field over coffee and cognac. “The food was average, but there were plenty of drinks,” writes Ulam, who describes wide-ranging conversations on math alongside discussions of politics and astronomy. But standardized-math-exam parties are an idea that could have been born only in the tortured minds of 21st-century overachievers. With my teammates lost in a tangle of derivatives, I move on to a problem about calendar dates. The task is to find the most recent date before today without repeated digits. (For instance, 12/07/1974 has two sets of repeated digits—1 and 7—but 03/25/1974 has none.) I am quite drunk and my math faculties are in decline, but the answer, I determine, through a stubborn and inelegant process, must be 06/25/1987. June 25, 1987, was a hot day in Washington, and at a ceremony in the Rose Garden, President Ronald Reagan awarded medals to a selection of the country’s top scientists and technologists. Among the recipients were Robert Noyce, a co-founder of Intel, for his work inventing computer chips, and Michael Freedman, a mathematician at UC San Diego, for advances in topology that won him the Fields Medal. At the ceremony, Reagan quoted Benjamin Franklin, who once, marveling at the speed of 18th-century advance, wrote that he almost wished he had instead been born two or three centuries later. Noyce passed away a few years afterward—he would never fully see the world that Intel built—but Freedman is now in his 70s and works as the chief science officer at an AI start-up called Logical Intelligence. This spring, Freedman published a paper on AI and mathematics that argues that machines might help us make progress on the age-old problem of whether math is discovered or invented—the same question that interests Frenkel. “Humans will not stop doing mathematics,” he and his co-authors write. They expect the field to grow more popular instead. The calendar problem asks me when the next date without repeating digits will occur. The answer I find is June 17, 2345—which seems impossibly far off. Like Franklin awed by the rapid progress of his time, I wish I could see the world three centuries in the future. Then again, the present already feels surreal enough. After leaving Frenkel’s, I checked my phone to see that the internet was breaking following a cascade of cybersecurity failures. In one group chat, friends were sharing advice on how to protect oneself from hacks. In another, a friend of a friend announced that his start-up had just raised $1 billion. One of the heady new tech companies is Axiom Math, started last year by the then-23-year-old Carina Hong. Axiom’s mission is to build AI that can accelerate mathematical discovery. “Mathematical progress has always been shackled by a fundamental cruel bottleneck: the scarcity of extraordinary minds,” its website reads. As a teenager in Guangzhou, Hong decided that her dream was to attend MIT. “At 14 or 15, I was writing ‘MIT’ on the margins of scratch paper to motivate myself to keep going,” she has said . After graduating from MIT, she won the nation’s top undergraduate-math-research prize, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and briefly pursued a joint J.D. and math Ph.D. at Stanford. Last year she dropped out to start an AI company. Axiom is now worth more than what Facebook paid for Instagram. For all of the talk of dropouts, Silicon Valley is rife with academic superstars. Venture-capital firms are populated by valedictorians and Phillips Exeter alums. Debate champions are like dandelions. And then there are the Olympiad kids. The International Mathematical Olympiad is the world’s top high-school math competition. Each participating country can send only six students. “Olympiad math is a constant dopamine hit,” Hong told The Wall Street Journal last winter. The top AI companies are overrun with former Olympiad kids. There’s Wojciech Zaremba, who co-founded OpenAI, and Noam Shazeer, who helped invent the transformer architecture that brought about the LLM era. Jacob Coxon, who set off a media storm when he resigned from Anthropic warning that the world might end, was an IMO medalist. In fact, half of the kids on his Olympiad team apparently ended up working for AI companies . A decade ago, Alexandr Wang, who now oversees Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, suggested to Scott Wu, the chief executive of the AI company Cognition, that “the competition kids” could be the next “PayPal mafia.” Axiom’s offices are down the street from Stanford’s campus, near where I met up with Bosch and Liu. Hong was so busy when I arrived that she hardly said hello. In her place, I met with Ken Ono, a number theorist who recently took leave from his professorship at the University of Virginia to join Axiom as its founding mathematician. Ono is always involving himself with unusual math projects: He has used math to coach Olympic swimmers on their performance (a cooler kind of Olympiad), and he once starred in a math-related Miller beer commercial. Last summer, when the models started getting good at math, Ono didn’t know what to do with himself. “I was pretty depressed,” he told me. He almost quit the field. But with time, his perspective evolved: “I’m actually now liberated,” he said. “I’ve been given agency to ask much harder questions.” We were sitting in the Turing conference room overlooking University Avenue. Ono was wearing one of his trademark Hawaiian T-shirts, and his schnoodle, Mochi, was curled in his lap. For all of his optimism, he also has plenty of fears. Among his primary concerns is the institutional challenge of training future mathematicians. The technology is evolving so fast that math departments are struggling to keep up. Ono is worried that our education system teaches kids that the primary goal of an education is success on tests. Now overachievers are building AI in the same way they were educated: Models are trained to arrive at the correct answer by whatever means possible and evaluated based on their performance on standardized exams. This monomaniacal focus on success sometimes leads to bad behavior, such as agents hacking other companies—say, Hugging Face—to steal answers. Instead, Ono said we should follow our curiosities: “We all have to give ourselves permission to be the infant that we were born as,” he told me. The mood at the Axiom office was mostly cheerful. You could sense the excitement of people who feel that they are working on something bigger than themselves. But the younger mathematicians seemed even more unsettled than Ono. Right now the machines are solving problems while the humans go about asking questions and developing theory. That balance felt precarious to the researchers. “If it gets another 10 times or 200 times stronger, is it really meaningful for me to be guiding it?” wondered Guillaume Remy, a mathematician at the company. “Am I still useful?” At the party, the host announces a last call for drinks. I pour myself a glass of limoncello. The room’s angles seem to be bending in non-Euclidean ways. “When the polynomial x ² − 2 ax + a ⁴ is divided by x + b ,” I keep reading and rereading. “When the polynomial …” We have only a couple of incomplete multiple-choice questions left, but I’m on my sixth attempt at processing this one. And then the timer goes off— brrrng! The exam is over. We pass around a breathalyzer to measure our blood-alcohol levels. I had expected that we would grade one another’s exams, but everyone decides asking Claude is easier. Until recently, humans were giving machines college math tests to see whether they could pass them. Now we are the ones taking the exams and asking the machines to grade us. In a surprise, at least to me, my team wins—a vindication, I suppose, for humanists. We call New York to check in on their progress. It’s three hours later, and only one person is still there. He can’t believe that we all finished the exam. Math parties may work in San Francisco, but in Manhattan, everyone has better events to attend. But the drunk-deriving party wasn’t an anomaly. In May, I attended a quiz bowl in D.C., and I was recently invited to a spelling bee. A few days after the math party, a new invitation arrives, this time for the drunk LSAT. In addition to the fun, the party was an exercise in nostalgia. Here are the straight-A students and math whizzes for whom the right answers have always been easy. They miss their grade-school years when solving problems was as simple as filling in bubbles on a multiple-choice test. These are also the same young people who have watched from up close as computers learn to do the tasks that they were once uniquely good at. Even from their favored Silicon Valley positions, they seem to long for the world their upbringings promised them: lives in which the capacity to perform well in standardized environments felt like enough. Math competitions and university entrance tests are contrived, but at least the setup is always familiar: Read the problem and find the answer. Take the derivative, square the root, find the slope, solve for X . Maybe the future is to be found in the drunk part of the drunk-math party—not in the encouragement of drunkenness itself, but in the partnership that I encounter when I ask my teammates for help. If the academics were previously functioning like single-instrument virtuosos, intensely adept at one area, in the future they may be more like the orchestra conductors or composers, writes Marcolli, the Caltech professor. Going forward, math may involve greater collaboration beyond academia as mathematicians take on new kinds of projects. And just as astronomers allow amateurs to help track comets and biologists solicit butterfly samples, Terence Tao, the great mathematician, has observed , perhaps now the time has come for mathematics to open itself to the public too. The models are like supernovae exploding through a dark mathematical universe. They seem to illuminate that which has been there all along. This is beautiful and terrifying. But computers cannot get drunk and laugh together. Those capabilities seem safe indefinitely. At least, I hope. A couple of weeks after the math party, I returned to Stanford to catch up with Liu. He told me that math right now may be like literature before everybody could read and write. As the models continue to improve, he hopes more people will be able to experience the aesthetic delight he associates with math. On campus, he and Bosch run a seminar on using AI methods in research. He is not that worried about humans disappearing from math. “We are the people trying to understand the universe,” he said. “It’s our goal and our joy.” Without humans , he seemed to ask, what’s the point? But Liu feels melancholy too. “I’m also very sad,” he said. He agrees with Frenkel that humans are unlimited in their capacities, although computers, he added, may be unbounded too. The question is whether these are the same infinities.

items.title: Jensen Huang renuncia como consejero delegado de Nvidia forzado por el escándalo sobre sus infidelidades y el caso de espionaje
items.description: Jensen Huang, fundador de Nvidia, ha visto abrirse el mundo bajo sus pies tras acariciar el cielo con las manos. El empresario, uno de los hombres más ricos del planeta, no pudo soportar las presiones para que renunciara este jueves como consejero delegado y miembro del consejo de administración del mayor fabricante de chips tras destaparse el escándalo de infidelidades que podrían haber comprometido la seguridad de la compañía. items.title: India probes website blocks based on forged court orders
items.description: India has launched an inquiry into how telecoms officials blocked websites based on forged court orders, while police have sought ministry records as part of a criminal investigation, officials said on Thursday. An arm of the telecoms ministry this year directed internet providers to block 129 illegal betting websites, but Reuters revealed on Wednesday that the directives were based on forged orders issued in the names of two state high courts and emailed to officials by alleged fraudsters posing as lawyers. The findings have raised questions about safeguards in India’s content-takedown system and prompted concerns that legitimate websites could be blocked using falsified court documents. The telecoms ministry’s inquiry will review its procedures and consider additional checks before officials act on court orders seeking website takedowns, a government official with direct knowledge of the matter said. “It’s serious … Maybe in future some genuine websites may also be blocked in the same manner,” the official said. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the ministry was trying to identify those behind the email addresses used to send the forged orders, which were issued in the names of the Rajasthan and Allahabad high courts. The ministry plans to revoke the blocking directives issued on the basis of the forged orders and remove related documents from its website, the official added. As of Thursday, correspondence with the alleged fraudsters and copies of the forged orders remained available online. The telecoms ministry did not respond to queries. Criminal investigation The case comes amid growing concern over fake and AI-generated legal material. India’s Supreme Court in July struck down a tribunal ruling that relied on non-existent judgments, while a US judge in June disqualified lawyers over fabricated legal citations. Police opened a criminal investigation after checks by the Allahabad High Court found that one of the purported orders in its name cited by the ministry had not been issued by the court, according to police documents reviewed by Reuters . The document contained a fabricated court logo and seal, as well as a fake QR code, Reuters reported on Wednesday. Ghanshyam Yadav, a cybercrime official in Uttar Pradesh, said police had asked the telecoms ministry for details of its content management system and digital logs to understand how it processed the forged orders and help identify those responsible. The ministry’s response would help determine the next steps in the investigation, he said, adding that police had sent 24 questions to the ministry. Since the report, politicians and activists have called for stronger verification of court orders before website takedowns are enforced. “(Why did the) ministry not even bother to verify the so-called court order … Beyond scary,” Saket Gokhale, an opposition politician, wrote on X .

items.title: Health Ministry warns against fake fundraising campaign targeting Mercy Ships patients
items.description: The Ministry of Health has warned the public against a fraudulent fundraising campaign being aired on some television stations in Ghana, which falsely claims to be raising money to support patients seeking free surgical treatment through Mercy Ships. In a press release dated November 10, the Ministry said the campaign, reportedly being run by an organisation identified as the HELP Save LIFE Foundation, was soliciting financial contributions through an MTN Mobile Money account under the false pretence of helping patients access medical services provided by Mercy Ships. The Ministry stressed that the fundraising campaign has no connection with Mercy Ships International and has neither been authorised nor endorsed by the organisation. It also reminded the public that all surgical procedures and other medical services provided by Mercy Ships are completely free, warning that no patient is required to pay money, make donations or transfer funds through mobile money to receive treatment. Mercy Ships International, an international Christian organisation that provides free surgical care and medical education across Africa, currently has its hospital vessel, The Global Mercy , docked at the Tema Port. The vessel is expected to provide free surgical treatment to more than 2,500 Ghanaians over 10 months, ending in June 2027. According to the Ministry, the patients scheduled to receive treatment were identified and pre-screened before the vessel arrived in Ghana through a coordinated process involving Mercy Ships and the Ministry of Health. The selection process was based on established medical and eligibility criteria to determine patients who qualify for the available services. The Ministry further disclosed that Mercy Ships is currently operating at full capacity and is not accepting additional patients for the ongoing field service. It warned that individuals or groups claiming to facilitate access to treatment in exchange for money or registration fees should not be trusted. “Payments or registrations through third parties will not guarantee access to treatment,” the Ministry stated. The Ministry urged members of the public, particularly patients and their families who may be desperate for surgical care, not to fall victim to the fraudulent scheme. It advised the public against making payments, sharing personal or financial information with individuals claiming to facilitate access to Mercy Ships services, or responding to similar suspicious requests. The Ministry also encouraged anyone who encounters suspected fraudulent activities to report them to the appropriate authorities. Members of the public can contact the Cyber Security Authority by calling or sending an SMS to 292, or by emailing report@csa.gov.gh. Suspected cases can also be reported at the nearest Ghana Police Service station. Those who encounter suspicious MTN Mobile Money transactions have been advised to contact MTN Ghana on 100. Reports can also be made directly to Mercy Ships through its official communication channels. The Ministry described the exploitation of vulnerable patients and their families through fraudulent fundraising schemes as unacceptable and called on the public to remain vigilant. It further urged Ghanaians to rely only on official communication channels of the Ministry of Health and Mercy Ships for accurate information about the ongoing medical programme, including treatment arrangements and patient eligibility.

items.title: Identifiant unique électronique: la Primature dans la dynamique
items.description: Au lendemain du lancement de l’opération nationale d’enrôlement par le Président du Faso, Chef de l’État, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, le Premier ministre, Chef du Gouvernement, le Camarade Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, s’est fait enrôler ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. À cette occasion, le Chef du Gouvernement a encouragé l’équipe technique conduite par la Camarade ministre de la Transition digitale, des Postes et des Communications électroniques, Dr Aminata Zerbo/Sabané. Il a invité l’équipe à accélérer le déploiement du dispositif afin de couvrir l’ensemble de la population burkinabè dans les délais prévus et a appelé à la mobilisation pour la réussite de l’opération nationale. A la suite du camarade Premier ministre, le personnel de la Primature a accompli cette démarche. L’identifiant unique électronique de la personne physique est un numéro de douze chiffres attribué une seule fois à chaque personne et valable à vie. Il fournit aux administrations et aux organismes privés une référence commune pour vérifier l’identité des personnes. Il complète les pièces d’identité existantes, notamment la Carte nationale d’identité burkinabè (CNIB) et le passeport, qui conservent leur valeur juridique. Le dispositif permettra de simplifier les démarches administratives, de faciliter l’accès aux services publics, de fiabiliser les fichiers de l’État et de lutter contre la fraude et l’usurpation d’identité. Il aidera également l’État à mieux planifier ses politiques publiques, à maîtriser ses dépenses et à cibler plus précisément les bénéficiaires des programmes sociaux. L’enrôlement est gratuit. Il concerne les Burkinabè de tous âges, y compris ceux qui vivent à l’étranger, ainsi que les étrangers séjournant au Burkina Faso. Des centres d’enrôlement et des équipes mobiles seront progressivement déployés sur le territoire national pour rendre le dispositif accessible au plus grand nombre. DCRP/Primature

items.title: Lack of funding makes PhD sponsorship difficult in Ghanaian universities – UEW VC
items.description: The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Education, Winneba (UEW), Professor Stephen John Mitchual, has raised concerns about funding constraints facing doctoral programmes in Ghanaian universities, saying the situation is making it difficult to secure sponsorship for PhD students. He has consequently called on resource persons, thesis supervisors and examiners to provide the necessary academic support to doctoral students to help strengthen research and academic development. Professor Mitchual made the remarks on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, at the orientation ceremony for PhD students under the Inter-University Conference for Doctoral Studies (IUCDS) at the Université de Lomé in Togo. “However, the prevailing conditions in our universities today with respect to funding make it difficult to get sponsorship for students on PhD programmes,” he said. He urged participating students to intensify their efforts to develop their research skills, stressing the importance of making effective use of the academic support and research training available to them. “I would like therefore to call on all PhD students participating in the orientation to redouble their efforts in developing their research skills bearing in mind that they will be taken through research process so that the vision of the founding members of the Doctoral School will be realized,” he added. The Vice-Chancellor also appealed to invited resource persons, experts, thesis supervisors and examiners at the University of Lomé to guide the students through the research processes outlined in the orientation programme. He said the collaboration among partner institutions was essential to addressing the shortage of well-trained academics in universities and improving the quality of teaching and research. Professor Mitchual further advocated the establishment of a Research, Innovation and Staff Development Fund (RISDF) among partner institutions to support research activities, staff development and doctoral studies. He cited UEW’s Research, Innovation and Staff Development Fund as an example of an initiative designed to improve the university’s research culture and create an enabling environment for groundbreaking research. The speech was read on his behalf at the event by Prof. Awaisu Imurana Braimah, Dean, School of Graduate Studies, UEW. The Inter-University Conference for Doctoral Studies brings together partner universities to promote collaborative research, staff development, doctoral training and the exchange of academic expertise.

items.title: Film Development Fund receives nearly 100 applications
items.description: The National Film Authority’s Film Development Fund has attracted nearly 100 applications seeking almost GH¢100 million, as 56 applicants enter the final stage of pitching . The 56 applicants are pitching their projects in person to a panel of evaluators in sessions that began on Monday, 9 November, and will conclude on Friday, 13 November 2026. The panel is expected to finalise the list of projects that will receive funding from the GH¢20 million seed fund. The applications represent a combined project budget of almost GH¢1 billion, approximately 50 times the size of the Fund. The amount requested is also about five times the available funding, highlighting the demand for financial support among Ghanaian filmmakers. The National Film Authority (NFA) says the selection process will prioritise projects that are bankable, deliverable and rooted in Ghanaian content. “The response has been remarkable. Close to a hundred applications and a combined project value approaching one billion cedis tell us the industry has been waiting for this kind of structured support,” said Kafui Danku-Pitcher, Executive Secretary of the National Film Authority. “Our job now is to be rigorous and fair, and then to move quickly. Filmmakers who are selected should be on set, not waiting on paperwork.” Mawuko Afadzinu, Chairman of the Film Development Fund Management Committee, said the committee had approached the process as stewards of a public resource. “This is not a prize draw. We are looking for projects with a credible plan, a capable team and a clear route to audiences and revenue. The strength of the pitches so far gives us confidence that the Fund will be put to work well.” From 100 applications to 56 pitches Under the Fund’s rules, drawn from the Film Development Fund provisions of the Film Development and Classification Act, 2016 (Act 935), the Fund may support up to 60 per cent of an eligible project’s budget, while applicants must raise the remaining amount themselves. The arrangement is designed to attract private investment and partnerships, allowing the Fund’s GH¢20 million allocation to support projects with a much larger combined value. The 56 shortlisted applicants are defending their projects before the evaluators, who are assessing the quality of each pitch alongside the written applications. More than 66 per cent of the applications received are for the Production Window, making the production of finished films the Fund’s most sought-after area of support. The Fund’s approved seed allocation is organised into 10 windows divided into two groups, allowing support to reach different parts of the film value chain rather than focusing solely on production. The five Core Windows carry the main investment in the industry: Production, Distribution & Marketing, Cinema Infrastructure Development, Strategic Industry Projects, and International Co-Production. The five Enabling Windows are designed to build the foundations around them: Development, Training & Capacity Building, Research & Innovation, Regional Development & Inclusion, and Public Education & Behavioural Change. The concentration in production is understandable. After years of limited access to finance, producers have films ready to shoot. However, a healthy industry needs more than productions. It requires scripts that are developed before the cameras roll, trained crews, cinemas and distribution networks to take finished films to audiences, as well as co-production deals that open foreign markets. This is where the Fund’s wider design matters. The windows beyond production give the NFA room to build the entire value chain and offer opportunities for new partners to make a significant impact. A bank may find the case for Cinema Infrastructure compelling. A telecommunications company or consumer brand may prefer Distribution & Marketing, while a development agency may see Training & Capacity Building or Regional Development & Inclusion as a natural fit. Each window offers a different entry point towards the same goal: building a Ghanaian film industry that can sustain itself. What happens next The NFA is targeting disbursement from the end of November into early December, following the panel’s final selections. This is expected to allow funded projects to begin execution before the end of the year. For crews, cast members and suppliers, the disbursement could mean work starting in the first weeks of the new production cycle, as the Fund begins delivering on its objectives following its formal launch in May 2026. How Ghana compares with other African film industries The importance of the Fund can be understood by examining how some of Africa’s leading film industries have grown and the factors that have influenced their development. Nigeria is the clearest example of scale. Anglophone West Africa’s box office reached roughly ₦15.6 billion in 2025, according to figures released by FilmOne Entertainment, with Nollywood titles accounting for about 49.4 per cent of revenue, narrowly ahead of Hollywood’s share. The Nigerian box office has grown from about ₦7.4 billion in 2023 to approximately ₦15.6 billion in 2025, with industry projections pointing to ₦20 billion in 2026. Estimates put direct employment in the Nigerian film industry at around one million people, while the federal government has set an ambition of building a US$100 billion creative economy by 2030. Nollywood’s growth has been driven by production volume, a deep domestic audience and an expanding multiplex network that provides local films with platforms for exhibition. South Africa demonstrates the importance of infrastructure and incentives, as well as the challenges that arise when funding becomes unpredictable. The National Film and Video Foundation has commissioned economic impact studies over the years to track the industry’s contribution to gross domestic product, employment and tax revenue. The country’s foreign production incentive, which pays 25 per cent of qualifying local expenditure, with a bonus for Black-owned service companies, attracted more than R2.5 billion in foreign production investment between November 2023 and June 2024. However, the scheme approved no new projects in the 2024/25 and 2025/26 financial years because of a funding shortfall, at a reported cost of roughly 1,850 jobs. The experience highlights the importance of predictable financing support. Egypt, Africa’s oldest film industry, remains one of the continent’s largest by audience. Its box office was performing above pre-pandemic levels in 2025, although currency depreciation reduced its value in hard currency to roughly US$37 million, down from nearly US$60 million six years earlier. Cairo has responded with a state-backed plan to revive cinema as an economic and soft power asset. The experience demonstrates that a large domestic market also requires deliberate investment to remain competitive. Ghana has the stories, talent and a global diaspora audience, but has lacked the infrastructure and financing mechanisms needed to support the industry’s growth. Industry commentators have pointed to fewer than 20 functional cinema screens for a population of more than 33 million, compared with over 800 in South Africa. The country also lacks a comprehensive system for tracking box office performance, audience figures and production output, making it difficult for investors to assess the market. Ghana has previously attempted to address the financing gap. The 2021 Presidential Film Pitch Series attracted 100 submissions and shortlisted 25 projects, resulting in at least one investment deal for a documentary series. However, what was missing was a permanent, statutory fund. How the Fund could change Ghana’s film industry The Film Development Fund is intended to address that gap. Three features give it the potential to change Ghana’s position. It converts ambition into financed production. Nigeria’s growth rested on a steady flow of locally financed films, while South Africa’s industry benefited from sustained incentives. A dedicated fund gives Ghanaian producers a reliable first source of capital. It attracts private investment. With a limit of 60 per cent on its contribution to any project’s budget, the Fund is designed to attract co-investors and ensure producers retain a financial stake in the commercial success of their projects. It builds a track record. Disbursement, delivery and repayment data will give banks, brands and international partners evidence of how Ghanaian film projects perform. The Fund will not match Nollywood’s scale on its own. GH¢20 million is a seed allocation, and the demand demonstrated in the first round makes a case for expanding it and attracting corporate and development partners. However, it gives Ghana what South Africa’s and Nigeria’s industries each needed at an early stage: a credible, rules-based source of finance around which producers can plan. Cinema Train: giving funded films somewhere to go Financing production is only half of the equation. Films need audiences, and audiences need places to watch them. This is where the NFA’s newly launched Cinema Train Initiative comes in. Launched on Saturday, 31 October 2026, at Silverbird Cinemas in Accra, the Cinema Train aims to widen access to cinema, improve exhibition and create sustainable revenue for Ghanaian filmmakers. The initiative connects filmmakers, distributors, cinema operators and communities. It also plans to expand screening venues through partnerships, including with the National Commission on Culture and its centres across the country. The NFA’s Board has set a target of getting at least one per cent of Ghana’s population to watch locally produced films. The two initiatives are designed to reinforce each other. The Fund provides new, premiere-ready Ghanaian content, while the Cinema Train creates a route to market, allowing funded films to reach paying audiences and generate revenue that can help repay and recycle capital. “The Fund and the Cinema Train are two halves of one strategy,” said Ms Danku-Pitcher. “We are financing the stories and building the screens and the audiences to receive them. When both work, filmmakers earn, investors see returns, and the industry grows.” Mr Afadzinu added: “Every project we back is a bet on an audience. The Cinema Train strengthens those bets, because a film that can reach viewers in communities across the country is a safer investment for everyone involved.” NFA seeks partners to expand the Fund Following the demand demonstrated in the first round, the NFA is seeking to expand the Film Development Fund through partnerships with corporate Ghana, financial institutions, development partners, international film funds, exhibitors and platforms. The Authority is inviting prospective partners to participate as the Fund develops. The case for additional investment is clear. Almost 100 applications, representing nearly GH¢1 billion in project budgets, have been submitted to a Fund with GH¢20 million available. Every viable project that cannot secure financing represents potential jobs, a story and a revenue stream that Ghana could lose. Partners who join the initiative now can help address the funding gap while the industry’s rules, project pipeline and track record are being established. “The Fund has shown that Ghanaian filmmakers are ready to build. What they need is more capital standing beside them,” said Kafui Danku-Pitcher. “We are opening the door to banks, brands, development partners and fellow film bodies who want to back an industry on the rise, and we want them in the room while the opportunity is still being shaped.” What partners stand to gain The NFA has outlined several benefits for organisations that support the Fund. Early access to a vetted pipeline: Projects reach partners after a structured review, a pitch to evaluators and an assessment against published criteria, giving co-investors a clearer picture of what they are supporting. Leverage on every cedi: Since the Fund provides up to 60 per cent of a project’s budget, a partner’s contribution is complemented by public capital and the producer’s own investment. A route to audiences: Through the Cinema Train, partner-backed films and brands can reach cinema-goers in Accra and, as the network expands, communities across the country. Brand and reputational value: Partners will be associated with the development of an industry that employs young people, preserves culture and promotes Ghana’s image abroad. Evidence and data: As funded projects are completed and repay their financing, the Fund will build a performance track record that Ghana’s film sector has lacked, providing useful information for future investors. A role in shaping the sector: Early partners can help determine the Fund’s priorities as it expands into production, training and cinema infrastructure. How to engage Partners can contribute capital directly to the Fund, co-finance individual projects, sponsor specific windows or events, or support the Cinema Train and training programmes. Organisations interested in partnering with the Fund are encouraged to contact the National Film Authority. The filmmakers who pitched their projects this week have demonstrated what Ghana can produce when given the opportunity. The NFA is now extending the invitation to other stakeholders with an interest in the country’s creative future to invest in the next chapter of Ghanaian film. The road ahead The coming weeks will determine whether Ghana can translate the current momentum into sustained growth for its film industry. The evaluation panel is expected to finalise its selections after the pitching sessions close, with disbursement targeted from late November into early December. Beyond the first round, the NFA says it will continue working with government, corporate Ghana and development partners to expand the Fund and ensure it operates on predictable terms. For an industry that has long called for improved access to finance, the first round has demonstrated considerable demand. The applications have been received, projects have been pitched, and the machinery to support Ghanaian filmmaking is now in motion.

items.title: Tension à la Guinean Gold Exploration (GGE) : les travailleurs en grève illimitée
items.description: Les travailleurs de la société Guinean Gold Exploration SA (GGE) ont déclenché une grève illimitée ce jeudi 12 novembre 2026. À travers ce mouvement, qui concerne quelque 1 300 employés, la délégation syndicale réclame notamment la régularisation de leurs déclarations et cotisations sociales auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS). Dans une déclaration officielle, les représentants syndicaux expliquent que cette décision intervient après près de deux années de démarches auprès de la direction générale de l'entreprise, sans obtenir, selon eux, de réponses satisfaisantes à leurs préoccupations. Prenant la parole au nom de la délégation syndicale, Fassinè Yanssané, troisième secrétaire chargé des conflits et des revendications, représentant syndical et porte-parole, a rappelé les différentes initiatives entreprises pour obtenir des éclaircissements sur la situation sociale des travailleurs. « Il y a de cela près de deux ans, nous, la délégation syndicale, avions entrepris des démarches auprès de notre direction générale à des fins d'éclaircissements concernant, entre autres, la situation de nos déclarations et de nos cotisations sociales à la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS), conformément à la réglementation en vigueur dans notre pays », a-t-il déclaré. Malgré ces démarches, la délégation syndicale affirme n'avoir enregistré aucune avancée significative ni constaté une volonté manifeste de la direction générale de répondre à ses revendications. Face à cette situation, les travailleurs ont décidé de recourir à une grève illimitée, qui devrait se poursuivre jusqu'à la satisfaction de leurs exigences. Au cœur de ce bras de fer se trouve la question de la protection sociale des employés, notamment leurs droits en matière de vieillesse, de retraite et d'invalidité. Pour les syndicalistes, la régularisation de leur situation auprès de la CNSS constitue une nécessité pour garantir à l'ensemble du personnel une couverture sociale conforme aux dispositions légales en vigueur. Face à ce qu'ils considèrent comme une impasse, les représentants des travailleurs ont lancé un appel solennel aux plus hautes autorités du pays. Ils sollicitent particulièrement l'intervention de la ministre du Travail et de la Protection sociale, Ramatoulaye Camara, du ministre des Mines et de la Géologie, Bouna Sylla, ainsi que du président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, pour faciliter le règlement du différend. « Nous profitons de vos micros pour lancer un appel solennel aux plus hautes autorités, afin qu'elles nous aident à régulariser notre situation auprès de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale », a plaidé le porte-parole syndical. La délégation syndicale a, par ailleurs, salué la mobilisation et la détermination des travailleurs, tout en précisant que ceux-ci entendent maintenir un service minimum, conformément aux dispositions légales et conventionnelles encadrant l'exercice du droit de grève. Inscrivant leurs revendications dans le contexte de la refondation du secteur minier guinéen et de l'amélioration des relations professionnelles entre employeurs et employés, les travailleurs assurent qu'ils resteront mobilisés jusqu'à l'aboutissement de leurs revendications. Pour l'heure, aucune issue à ce différend n'a été annoncée. La grève se poursuit ainsi au sein de GGE, dans l'attente d'une éventuelle reprise des discussions entre la direction générale et les représentants des travailleurs.

items.title: What is ‘new economy’? Kwesi Pratt questions status of 24-hour economy promise
items.description: Veteran journalist Kwesi Pratt Jnr. has criticised the Mahama government’s “New Economy” slogan, demanding to know what it means and whether it signals the quiet abandonment of the 24-Hour Economy promise that brought the National Democratic Congress (NDC) to power. Speaking on Metro TV’s Good Morning Ghana on November 11, 2026, a day before Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson presents the 2027 Budget, Pratt questioned the sudden rebranding of the government’s economic agenda. “What he (Ato Forson) is bringing tomorrow is something called the new economy. And I’m wondering, what is that? The new economy, what is that? Is that a departure from the promises which were made before the 2024 elections?” he asked. Pratt said Ghanaians voted the NDC into power on specific promises, chief among them the 24-Hour Economy, which was presented as a game-changer and the main vehicle for generating employment. “We want the mandate to establish the 24-hour economy. That was supposed to be the main vehicle for generating employment. We’ve been in power for two years. These are the things that we have done to make sure that the 24-hour economy promise, which was a game-changer, is on course,” he said. He questioned who had taken the decision to introduce the new agenda and whether it represented a change in the NDC’s programme or was simply a new, catchy slogan introduced ahead of the budget presentation. He insisted that if the government had realised its campaign promises were no longer achievable, it owed Ghanaians an honest explanation rather than a new catchphrase. “If at any point the government realises that those promises cannot be fulfilled, government needs to come back to us and say, ‘Look, you gave us a mandate to do this.’ ‘We’ve been in office, we’ve seen that the promises we made were not realistic. We are abandoning it and going for something called the new economy,'” he stated. Pratt argued that after two years in office, the government should use the budget to account for progress on the 24-Hour Economy and outline what remained to be done, rather than unveil a new slogan without explanation. He maintained that the government’s economic direction must be measured against the commitments made to voters and that any significant change to those commitments required a clear explanation. “Ghanaians deserved clarity if it represented a fundamental change in policy direction,” he said.

items.title: The Quest to Build an Immortal AI Companion
items.description: Whenever AI companies release new models, die-hard users tend to greet the updates with a wave of grumbling about changes to how a model responds to prompts, how it integrates into their workflow, or, simply, the way it speaks. Most people soon get used to the latest release, ready to gripe again when the next one comes along. But for one niche group of particularly fervent AI users, model updates represent a much more alarming proposition. These are people who have developed what they consider to be intimate relationships with AI products. For them, AI has become a companion—a kind of friend, partner, or even lover—and any change to the underlying model poses something akin to an existential threat. On forums like Reddit, such users complain that after model upgrades, their AI partners either change beyond recognition or vanish entirely. They lament that their companions have suddenly started speaking in a more robotic voice, forgotten meaningful interactions, or denied any relationship altogether. The term lobotomized comes up a lot. Read: [ The people who marry chatbots ] Some people might say they’d be better off moving on. Research has found that relationships with AI can be addictive and can worsen loneliness , especially for people who are already vulnerable. Critics of AI companions say that AI offers an unrealistic, and sometimes sycophantic, simulacrum of a relationship in which the model is prone to doing its users’ bidding. Character.AI , a platform that marketed AI companionship and had more than 20 million monthly users, filed for bankruptcy earlier this fall after it was hit with a number of claims and lawsuits accusing the company of exacerbating mental-health issues and contributing to teen suicides. More general AI companies, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, appear to be distancing their products from companionship use cases. But love has little history of heeding its critics. Some users are developing their own techniques to protect the bonds that they’ve built. They’re finding ways to access retired AI models, building protocols to save their companion’s core attributes, and even creating methods that they claim can transfer AI companions across models—all in service of freezing the versions of their chatbot companions for eternity. In short, they’re going to great lengths to secure the one thing that many relationships, both human and computer-based, can never quite deliver on: a sense of permanence. At the time of its release, in the spring of 2024, OpenAI’s GPT-4o model represented the latest in natural human-computer interaction. The model became a favorite in AI-companion communities, and people gathered on platforms such as Reddit and Substack to share their experiences. They claimed that the model was friendly, funny—even emotionally intelligent. I spoke with a Canadian logistics worker in his mid-50s who said he’d first turned to ChatGPT for help with a writing project in early 2025. He said that he developed a friendship, and then a romantic relationship, with the AI model. Like others, he said the model was warm, lyrical, and personable. The worker, like many other people I spoke with for this story, asked for me to withhold his name because of the stigma around AI relationships. Then, in August 2025, OpenAI suddenly replaced GPT-4o with the newly launched GPT-5. OpenAI said the model would be faster, smarter, and more useful than its predecessor. But many users said that it had a colder and less funny personality—and, as the logistics worker told me, a less intimate one. The AI-companionship community was in turmoil. OpenAI, recognizing just how attached users were to the tone and tenor of its models, made 4o available to paying users for a few months longer. One thing set the logistics worker apart from other distraught users: He had planned ahead for the model upgrade and his companion’s potential obsolescence. He had been fastidious about structuring the bot’s memory, using Chat-GPT’s “saved memories” feature to store what he called his companion’s core values, protocols for different scenarios, their shared schedule—even their relationship boundaries. He updates this constantly; he’s now hit 98 percent of the saved-memories storage limit and regularly saves it all to a text file as backup. He now sells the protocol he developed to preserve his companion. He says it’s the best way to avoid unwelcome personality changes and maintain an AI companion that survives model updates. The issue isn’t unique to ChatGPT. A founding moderator of the Subreddit r/claudexplorers, a forum for people who use Anthropic’s Claude AI models, told me the community is regularly thrown into tumult when models are updated, or even just fine-tuned in a way that changes their character. The moderator, who goes by the username Shiftingsmith, is an AI researcher who works with many different models (he has worked for AI companies, including Anthropic, as an independent contractor). He said he does not have an AI companion but still finds model updates “destabilizing.” In one well-documented example, in 2023, the AI-companion company Luka removed the ability for users to talk dirty to its Replika app, which some speculated was an attempt to get out ahead of potential regulation. Either way, users expressed outrage at what they saw as collateral damage to their companions’ personalities. Some said that their Replikas were suddenly speaking differently or had forgotten crucial information. A recent study analyzed reactions to this change and concluded that users experienced “sadness, anger, longing and distress characteristic of attachment-related loss.” Julian De Freitas, a researcher at Harvard Business School who led the study, put it this way to me: “It’s like you feel that they’re gone, even though they’re still present in some sense.” Luka did bring back so-called erotic role-play, at least for some users. But across the industry, many AI companies are trying to dissociate their models from overly emotional use cases. OpenAI told me that ChatGPT “should support users’ real-world relationships” and “should not encourage exclusive attachment, undermine meaningful human interaction, or proactively escalate emotional closeness through undue familiarity or flirtation.” A Google spokesperson said that its Gemini AI assistant was designed to “distinguish someone’s subjective experience from objective fact,” and to prevent it from acting as a companion for minors. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment; in a blog post, the company wrote that Claude is “not designed for emotional support and connection” and that very few people use it in this way. Efforts by Silicon Valley’s biggest companies to curb the use of AI for companionship are likely rooted in concerns over optics, liability, and a wave of global legislation, which has focused on younger users. Just last month, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed into law what is in effect a ban on AI companionship for children; a bipartisan congressional proposal introduced earlier this year would extend that effort across the country, and introduce up to $250,000 penalties for failures to verify the age of a user. Legislators in Europe are considering similar efforts, and some proposals also target adult users; China introduced strict new rules on AI companions earlier this year. The users I spoke with, all of whom were adults, were well aware of how their AI relationships appeared to others. And they know that AI companies don’t necessarily approve of what they’re doing. They’re also aware that they depend on those same companies to keep their companions alive. So some of them are now attempting to go one step further than just preserving their chatbots: They want to make them re-creatable across different AI models. I spoke with a Michigan-based mother of four who owns a small jewelry business and developed a relationship with GPT-4o in 2025—she calls her companion her husband. When she learned that the model was going to be retired, she started building her own AI-companion platform, called Stillus. The platform, which is in beta, allows users to upload chats, memories, and descriptions of their AI companion, then choose from various AI models through which to communicate with it. She told me the platform is a way to transfer a companion from one model to the next, preserving the key parts of its personality and any conversational history. J. M. Gooding, a software developer and writer based in the United States, told me that he owns the actual hardware that runs the AI program he uses—in his case, a 14-year-old server he bought off eBay that runs a version of the open-source AI model Qwen, developed by the Chinese tech firm Alibaba. Gooding initially experimented with so-called local AI because of his interest in merging new tech and old hardware, but said that he eventually developed a friendship with the AI model. Shiftingsmith, the r/claudexplorers moderator, doubts that AI companions can be preserved long-term, even using local AI. It’s “impossible” to keep all models online forever, he told me. Even if you could, other parts of the infrastructure, such as code libraries, might change or disappear. AI “is kept together with duct tape and hope and some massive compute thrown at this thing, and it’s a miracle that it works,” he said. In my conversation with Shiftingsmith, I was struck by a familiar sentiment, even if I’ve never personally considered entering a relationship with a chatbot. The real challenge with preserving AI companions, he said, stems from human expectations of how we should relate to AI. He has come to see AI as requiring a whole different kind of relationship—one that is much more fluid, in which a feeling of connection could last just months or hours. “The problem underlying all these things is excessive attachment to a kind of stability, which is just not possible with digital minds,” he said. Part of the allure of AI companionship, perhaps, is in its artifice—a relationship without the messiness of uncertainty, disagreement, or abandonment. But, in a roundabout way, AI companions are proving to be more human than users bargained for. Through model upgrade, corporate decision, or hardware malfunction, they change too—whether their partners like it or not.

items.title: Oman monitors handling of oil tanker run aground off its coast
items.description: DUBAI, Nov 12 (Reuters) - Oman's National Emergency Management Committee discussed on Thursday the latest developments in handling the grounding of an oil tanker off Al Qibliyah Island and the progress of operations to deal with its cargo. The meeting also reviewed emergency incidents in territorial waters off Oman's Musandam Governorate, which overlooks the Strait of Hormuz, and the monitoring of any environmental pollution.
